The reproduction, searches, tests, and typecheck were rehearsed locally on October 16, 2026, with Node.js 24.10.0, npm 11.6.0, ripgrep 15.2.0, and ast-grep 0.51.0. The published repository was cloned and its starter revision verified. The supplied local folder and Git bundle also work for this guide.

Author: Saurabh Rob Dahal, Developer Advocate, AWS

Description: Investigate a TypeScript retry bug using repository mapping, ripgrep, ast-grep, symbol navigation, and an evidence note you can use with different coding assistants.

Level: Beginner · Time: 60 minutes with a facilitator, after setup

A coding assistant can suggest a plausible fix before it understands a repository. A useful investigation makes its reasoning checkable: where does the behavior live, what evidence explains it, and which checks would distinguish a correct fix from a partial one?

In this workshop, you will investigate one prepared bug. A client configured with maxRetries: 0 still makes three requests when its transport fails. You will follow that setting across files, ask an assistant for a supported explanation, and make a small change.

The bug is deliberately small. The practice is learning how to approach unfamiliar code without reading every file or accepting the first plausible explanation. The same approach is useful when an application setting behaves unexpectedly, a wrapper changes an argument, or an error originates in another package.

Each step answers a different question. If the evidence is incomplete, return to a focused lookup before editing.

You can follow along with Kiro, Codex, Claude Code, or another assistant that can read your project, run shell commands, and edit files. Choose a coding model supported by your tool. The exercise uses ordinary commands and a Markdown note, so it does not depend on a particular model, context window, or project-memory format.

Your editor supplies definition and reference navigation. No AWS account, credentials, or cloud deployment is required. If you are working independently, pause at the evaluation prompts and take the time you need.

Before the workshop

You need Git, Node.js 24 with npm, ripgrep, and an editor with TypeScript definition and reference navigation. You should be comfortable opening a terminal and editing a text file. Complete your chosen assistant's sign-in before the session.

The commands use a Bash-compatible shell: Terminal on macOS, a Linux terminal, or WSL on Windows. Run commands from the repository root unless a step says otherwise. Copy the contents of a command block without adding a leading $ prompt.

Install ripgrep using the official installation instructions. On a Mac with Homebrew:

brew install ripgrep

Use a fresh checkout. Choose one of these routes, then run the shared setup below. Clone the workshop starter repository:

git clone https://github.com/sdahal1/repo-search-workshop.git repo-search-workshop
cd repo-search-workshop

If you already have the supplied local folder, skip cloning and enter it:

cd repo-search-workshop

If you have repo-search-workshop.bundle in your current directory, create a checkout from that local Git bundle instead:

git clone --branch starter ./repo-search-workshop.bundle repo-search-workshop
cd repo-search-workshop

From the repository root, pin the workshop's starter revision and install its dependencies:

git checkout --detach 5280be1e6659942e2335b10bde88b1fccdf9b76d
git switch -c workshop/my-investigation
node --version
npm --version
rg --version
npm ci
npx --no-install ast-grep --version
git status --short

The checkout puts everyone on the same source revision. The new branch gives you a place to keep your work. The starter pins @ast-grep/cli to 0.51.0 as a development dependency. npm ci installs dependencies from the committed lockfile without updating it. npm ci documentation

Check your setup: Node should report version 24, ast-grep should report 0.51.0, and git status --short should produce no output in this fresh checkout. Open the entire repository folder in your editor so it can find the TypeScript project configuration.

The npx commands use the installed project executable. If npm offers to download a package, stop and check that installation succeeded and that you are in the repository root.

The starter provides a fake transport, a failing regression test, an investigation template, and a saved AST rule. A transport is the component that performs the underlying request. Here, a small local function stands in for it, records calls, and fails predictably. No real service is involved.

You may type each command yourself or ask the assistant to run the exact command. For the first pass, run the searches yourself so you can connect their inputs to their results. Later, delegate those same steps with an explicit scope.

1 Show the failure

Time: 0–4 minutes

Concept: A reproduction turns a report into an observable difference between expected and actual behavior. It also gives you a check to run after editing.

The report says: “I set maxRetries to zero, but the client still retries.” Before investigating, define what counts as a retry. In this project, it is an additional attempt after the initial request. Therefore:

total attempts when every request fails = 1 + allowed retries
zero retries = one initial attempt

Count transport calls, including the initial request. The symptom does not yet tell us which function is responsible.

Task: Run the demo, then the focused test:

npm run demo
npm run test:repro

Expected result before the fix: The demo records three transport calls for maxRetries: 0. The focused test fails because it expects one call and observes three. A failing assertion is intentional here; a missing-module or command-not-found error is a setup problem.

The local rehearsal confirmed this failure. The full starter suite ran 11 tests: 10 passed, and only the zero-retries reproduction failed. Typechecking passed before the fix, showing that this behavioral bug is not a type error.

Evaluate: Open packages/client/test/client.test.ts. Find where the test supplies zero to the public client API, where the fake transport increments its counter, and where the test checks the final count. Confirm that the test observes behavior through the public API rather than directly testing a helper expression.

Write the reproduction command, expected count, and actual count in workshop/INVESTIGATION.md. Do not change an assertion to match the current behavior.

Teaching moment: “The transport ran three times” is evidence. “The retry loop is off by one” is a hypothesis. Other explanations are possible: the option might be dropped, defaulted incorrectly, or interpreted differently. Keep those possibilities open until you trace the value.

2 Map the repository

Time: 4–12 minutes

Concept: A repository map identifies responsibilities and boundaries. It helps you choose where to look before spending time on implementation details.

Task: Run:

git ls-files
git ls-files 'README*' '*package.json' '*tsconfig*.json'
git ls-files 'packages/client/*'

The first command shows tracked paths. The next commands narrow that inventory to project descriptions, manifests, TypeScript configuration, and the client package. Quoting the patterns passes them to Git instead of asking the shell to expand them. git ls-files documentation

Open README.md, the root package.json, packages/client/package.json, and docs/client-options.md. Find the test scripts and the meaning of maxRetries. A manifest describes a package's dependencies, scripts, and entry points; it helps connect a folder to what the project runs.

Use the map to choose a starting area. The relationships must still be confirmed in source and tests.

Ask your assistant:

Map this repository using its tracked file paths, README, package
manifests, and docs/client-options.md. Do not edit files.

Identify the package most likely to own the reported retry behavior.
Explain your choice using paths and documented responsibilities.
Do not read every implementation file yet.

Expected result: packages/client is the likely owner. Its src directory contains implementation and its test directory contains the reproduction. The option documentation establishes that zero is valid.

Evaluate: Write one sentence explaining why the client package is relevant. “It has client in its name” is a starting clue. A documented responsibility and a reproduction that imports the package are stronger support.

Also identify the package's test command before editing. That prevents the assistant from guessing how the project is verified.

Teaching moment: A map is a working hypothesis about ownership. Expand your scope if imports lead elsewhere. git ls-files is an inventory of tracked files; it does not include every untracked file on disk, and it does not describe runtime behavior.

3 Search by text

Time: 12–18 minutes

Concept: Text search is useful when you know a name, error, or literal value. It finds mentions in code, tests, comments, and documentation.

Task: Search the owning package and option documentation:

rg -n -F 'maxRetries' packages/client docs/client-options.md
rg -n -C 3 -F 'maxRetries' packages/client/src

rg runs ripgrep. -n displays line numbers, -F treats the query as literal text, and -C 3 includes three surrounding lines. The final arguments select where to search. ripgrep guide

Expected result: Matches lead to the option type, request path, retry implementation, and regression test. Read a result as a location to inspect, not a complete explanation. Open the enclosing function when three surrounding lines are insufficient.

Choose the search that matches your question. These tools complement one another throughout an investigation.

Evaluate: Classify useful matches by their role:

Kind of match What to learn from it
Option definition Which values the API accepts
Caller or wrapper Whether the value is forwarded or transformed
Implementation How the value affects behavior
Test Which behavior is asserted
Documentation What behavior is promised

Add useful paths and symbols to your investigation note. Record actual line numbers from your checkout; the article does not prescribe fixed line numbers.

If the search returns nothing, first check spelling, case, and your directory. A zero-result search means no matching text was found in the searched scope. It does not prove the behavior is absent from the program.

Teaching moment: A matching name does not establish a call relationship. Two modules may declare independent variables with the same spelling. Text search finds candidates; symbol navigation will help you distinguish them.

4 Search by structure

Time: 18–23 minutes

Concept: An abstract syntax tree, or AST, represents code through syntax nodes and their relationships. An expression such as left || right has an operator and two operands. Structural search asks for that arrangement while allowing selected parts to vary. ast-grep core concepts

You already know the option's name. Now ask a second question: where does the code use an OR expression that might supply a fallback? This is useful when the same structure appears under different variable names or across multiple lines.

Task: Start with the operator as literal text:

rg -n -F '||' packages/client/src

Keep -F: the pipe character has special meaning in regular expressions. Then run the prepared structural query:

npx --no-install ast-grep run --lang ts \
  --pattern '$VALUE || $FALLBACK' packages/client/src

Here, run performs a one-time search, --lang ts selects TypeScript, and --pattern supplies the code shape. There is no rewrite argument, so this command does not modify code. ast-grep run reference

Understand the placeholders

$VALUE and $FALLBACK are metavariables that match syntax nodes. Leave those names in the command. Keep the single quotes so the shell passes the dollar signs unchanged instead of expanding shell variables. ast-grep quick start

For this candidate:

options.maxRetries || DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES

the left capture is options.maxRetries and the right capture is DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES. The names VALUE and FALLBACK are labels we chose; they do not tell ast-grep what the author intended.

The simplified tree shows what stays fixed—the OR operator—and what the metavariables can capture.

Compare matches and counterexamples

Consider these illustrative snippets. They explain the pattern; they are not claimed to be exact starter files.

const a = options.maxRetries || DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES;

const b = options.timeoutMs
  ||
  5000;

const allowed = isAdmin || isOwner;

// options.maxRetries || DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES
const explanation = "options.maxRetries || DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES";

const enabled = isReady && hasPermission;

The broad pattern matches the OR expressions assigned to a, b, and allowed. The multiline expression still has the requested shape. The comment and string are not executable OR expressions, and the final expression uses a different operator. ast-grep pattern syntax

isAdmin || isOwner is a valuable counterexample: it matches, but the boolean logic may be entirely correct. A syntax match is not a bug diagnosis. The tool does not know whether zero is meaningful to this particular API.

Narrow and save the query

Require the property name while leaving the object and right-hand expression variable:

npx --no-install ast-grep run --lang ts \
  --pattern '$OPTIONS.maxRetries || $FALLBACK' packages/client/src

Expected result: The candidate in packages/client/src/retry.ts remains. The object name can vary, so config.maxRetries || 2 also matches. However, this narrower pattern would miss options['maxRetries'] || 2 or a property read first assigned to a local variable. That is a reason to inspect the surrounding code, not a reason to search every possible expression at once.

The starter's workshop/defaulting.yml saves the broad query:

id: find-or-expressions
language: TypeScript
rule:
  pattern: $VALUE || $FALLBACK

Run it with:

npx --no-install ast-grep scan \
  --rule workshop/defaulting.yml packages/client/src

The rule gives the query a name and language so someone else can repeat it. ast-grep rule essentials

In the pinned starter, the broad query returns four candidates: the multiline request-label expression, the trace expression, the retry-input validation condition, and the retry-setting expression. The first three implement intentional behavior. The narrowed query returns only the candidate in retry.ts. Compare these results with the literal text search, which also finds mentions inside a comment and a string.

Evaluate: Explain why each relevant match deserves inspection. Compare what text search found with what the structural query found. Save the candidate and its enclosing symbol in your note.

Teaching moment: Structural search reduces ambiguity about code shape. It does not establish runtime values, symbol identity, or business intent. Those need different evidence.

5 Follow the symbols

Time: 23–28 minutes

Concept: Symbol navigation resolves an identifier to its declaration and finds uses of that declaration. It helps answer which function is actually involved when names repeat or imports are renamed.

For example, a module could import withRetry as runWithRetries. Searching only for the original name might find the import but miss calls written with the alias. Definition navigation can connect those uses through the project language service.

Task: In your editor:

  1. Open the reproduction test and use Go to Definition on createClient.
  2. In packages/client/src/client.ts, locate the request path and the call to withRetry.
  3. Use Go to Definition on withRetry to reach packages/client/src/retry.ts.
  4. Use Find References on its definition to inspect the callers.
  5. Inspect ClientOptions in packages/client/src/types.ts and compare it with the documented contract.

Use the editor's context menu or command palette to find these actions. The names and shortcuts can differ; for one concrete implementation, see TypeScript navigation in Visual Studio Code.

Confirm the arrows by navigating definitions and inspecting callers. The picture illustrates the starter's relationships; it is not a screenshot or a generated runtime trace.

Expected result: You can follow the option from the public client API to the retry implementation. Check whether the wrapper forwards zero unchanged before interpreting the defaulting expression.

Evaluate: Record the caller and callee paths and symbols. A reference result may be a declaration, import, or call. Read it before recording a call relationship. Navigation also does not prove that a branch executed during the reproduction; combine it with the test and implementation.

Teaching moment: Language Server Protocol, or LSP, standardizes communication for code intelligence. Editors can also provide TypeScript navigation through their own language-service integrations. The shared requirement here is working definition/reference navigation. There is no universal lsp terminal command, and your assistant does not need direct LSP access. LSP specification

6 Gather evidence before asking for a fix

Time: 28–36 minutes

Concept: A short investigation note separates observations from interpretations and makes your context portable. Another assistant or teammate can inspect the same evidence without reconstructing a long conversation.

Keep the evidence compact enough to review, but specific enough to reproduce and challenge.

Task: Complete workshop/INVESTIGATION.md:

# Investigation

## Observed behavior
Reproduction command:
Expected behavior:
Actual behavior:

## Repository area
Owning package and evidence:

## Relevant code
Paths, symbols, actual line numbers, and caller relationships:

## Constraints
Preserve the public API and omitted-option behavior.
Keep the fake transport and meaningful assertions.

## Root cause hypothesis
Leave blank until the next step.

## Proposed modification points
Leave blank until the next step.

## Verification
npm run test:repro
npm test
npm run typecheck
git status --short
git diff
git diff --check

An evidence entry might say, “The reproduction passes zero at the public API and observes three transport calls.” Attach the actual test location. A hypothesis would say, “A defaulting expression may replace zero before the loop runs.” Keeping these in different sections makes it easier to notice what remains unproven.

Include a short reason beside each source location. “This wrapper forwards the option” is more useful than a list of six paths with no explanation. Leave out unrelated search results and large copied files; the assistant can open the referenced code.

Evaluate: Could someone who missed the walkthrough reproduce the failure and locate the relevant expressions from your note? Could they tell which claims you observed and which still require checking?

Teaching moment: Good context is selected evidence with an explicit purpose. Paths and symbols help someone relocate it; line numbers identify positions in this checkout and may move after edits.

7 Explain the root cause before editing

Time: 36–43 minutes

Concept: A supported hypothesis connects the input, the transformation, and the observed output. Evaluate that connection before changing code.

Task: In a fresh or existing assistant conversation in the same checkout, paste:

Read workshop/INVESTIGATION.md. Do not edit files.

Inspect the referenced code and explain the failing behavior.
If evidence is missing, identify the next focused lookup needed.

Return:
- Your root-cause hypothesis.
- Supporting paths, symbols, and actual line numbers.
- Any uncertainty or competing explanation.
- The smallest proposed change and expected modified files.
- Tests that distinguish a correct fix from a partial fix.

Stop before editing.

You may use a plan or read-only mode if your tool provides one. The explicit instruction is still useful because it tells the assistant what deliverable you want at this stage.

Expected explanation: 0 || DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES selects the default because zero is falsy. With a default of two retries, the always-failing transport receives one initial call plus two retries. The ?? operator uses its fallback only for null or undefined, preserving zero. TypeScript nullish coalescing documentation

The operator table explains language behavior. Its null, false, and empty-string examples do not expand the client's numeric input contract.

For a text version of the diagram:

| Left value (x) | x \|\| 2 | x ?? 2 | API meaning here |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 2 | 0 | Valid: disable retries |
| undefined | 2 | 2 | Omitted option: use the default |
| 1 | 1 | 1 | Valid: allow one retry |
| null | 2 | 2 | Language example, outside the option type |
| false | 2 | false | Language example, outside the option type |
| '' | 2 | '' | Language example, outside the option type |

Neither operator validates input. The proposed change corrects defaulting for values already allowed by the API.

Evaluate: Check three links in the explanation:

  1. The public contract allows zero, and the wrapper delivers it unchanged.
  2. The identified expression replaces zero with the documented default of two.
  3. The retry loop interprets two as additional attempts, producing three total calls.

If one link is missing, perform the next focused lookup. An answer that simply recommends ?? has not yet explained the whole symptom. A proposed loop change also needs evidence that the loop itself is wrong.

Optional self-check in your terminal:

node -e 'console.log({ or: 0 || 2, nullish: 0 ?? 2 })'

The expected values are or: 2 and nullish: 0. This checks language behavior in isolation; it does not prove the repository's value follows that path. The earlier evidence establishes that connection.

Update the hypothesis and proposed modification sections of your note. Do not broaden the API to accept null, strings, or booleans just because the operator table includes them.

Teaching moment: Different models may phrase the explanation differently. Judge the evidence and predicted behavior. A useful hypothesis also tells you what you should observe after the fix.

8 Make the narrow change and verify it

Time: 43–56 minutes

Concept: A fix must correct the reported behavior and preserve the surrounding contract. Test results and diff review provide different parts of that evidence.

Task: After checking the explanation, tell the assistant:

Apply the smallest change supported by our investigation.
Preserve the public API and default retry behavior.
Keep the reproduction's original assertion intact.
Add focused regression coverage only where it is missing.
Do not refactor unrelated code or update dependencies.
Do not stage or commit the changes.
Run the verification commands in workshop/INVESTIGATION.md.
Report the modified files and actual results, including failures.

The expected production change is:

- const retries = options.maxRetries || DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES;
+ const retries = options.maxRetries ?? DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES;

If you are editing manually, make the same justified change in the editor. Avoid a global replacement of ||: other matches may intentionally use boolean logic or falsy-value defaults.

Run the checks yourself if the assistant has not run them:

npm run test:repro
npm test
npm run typecheck
npm run demo
git status --short
git diff
git diff --check

Evaluate the behavior

A useful test matrix checks the repaired boundary and nearby behavior that should remain valid.

With the fake transport failing on every attempt, verify:

Input Expected total transport calls after the fix Why check it
maxRetries: 0 1 Reproduces the reported boundary
Option omitted, default of 2 3 Preserves the default
maxRetries: 1 2 Preserves explicit positive values

Also preserve immediate success: when the first request succeeds, there should be one call, regardless of a larger retry allowance. A retry budget allows extra attempts after failure; it does not require them after success.

The rehearsed solution passed the reproduction, all 11 tests, and typechecking; its demo showed one call for zero retries. Those are the expected results for your fix. Read the test output rather than accepting a summary that says “looks good.” Check which command ran and whether it completed successfully.

Evaluate the change

Inspect every changed file. The investigation note is expected to change. Production edits should be limited to the justified implementation; test edits should strengthen coverage while preserving the reproduction's original assertion.

Ask why any dependency lockfile, public type, unrelated helper, or large formatting block changed. Such edits need their own justification. Also inspect untracked files reported by git status, because a normal diff does not display their contents.

git diff shows unstaged tracked changes. If you staged anything, also run git diff --cached. git diff --check checks whitespace errors; silence does not establish behavioral correctness. git diff documentation

Teaching moment: The reproduction checks the bug. Nearby tests check preserved behavior. Typechecking checks type compatibility. Diff review checks the scope and meaning of edits. A passing check cannot answer all four questions.

Finish with a reusable investigation

Time: 56–60 minutes

Explain the bug to a partner in three sentences: what failed, where the value changed meaning, and how you verified the fix. Point to evidence for each sentence.

Then name the question each tool answered. Text search found mentions. AST search found a code shape. Symbol navigation connected definitions and uses. Tests observed behavior. Your investigation note connected those findings into an explanation someone else could review.

On your next unfamiliar repository, start with a reproducible symptom and a small map. Choose searches according to the question you need answered. Expand the scope when the evidence requires it, and give your assistant a clear boundary between investigating and editing.

If a step behaves differently

Symptom Next check
rg is not found Install ripgrep, reopen the terminal, and run rg --version.
ast-grep is missing or the version differs Return to the repository root; confirm npm ci succeeded with development dependencies installed.
AST search has no matches Check the directory, TypeScript language flag, and single quotes. Confirm you still have the unfixed starter.
Definition navigation fails Open the repository root, install dependencies, and confirm the editor recognizes the TypeScript project. Follow imports manually while fixing navigation.
The reproduction already passes Inspect the checkout and existing diff. You may have the solution or a previous edit. Preserve your work and use a fresh starter checkout.
A test reports a setup error Resolve that error before interpreting it as evidence of the retry bug.
The assistant edits during investigation Inspect the diff before continuing. Preserve your note and use a fresh starter checkout if needed.
The fix passes one test but breaks another Compare the failing case with the documented contract; revisit the hypothesis instead of weakening an assertion.

No cloud resources are created by this exercise, so there is no AWS cleanup step. Keep your checkout to reuse the investigation note and commands.

articles.title: Translation Is Not Agreement: Build a Clarification Handshake for Multilingual Chat
articles.description: Machine translation can make a group message readable without making its intent certain. Build a reproducible TypeScript clarification workflow for Tencent RTC Social Messaging with author-only answers, revision checks, explicit notification failures, and verification tests.
articles.body_html:
A multilingual chat can translate every word correctly and still leave someone wondering: Was that a suggestion, a deadline, or a polite refusal?

That uncertainty is not evidence that you are bad at communication—or that translation has failed. Natural languages encode tone, obligation, and context differently. The engineering mistake is treating translated text as if it removed those trade-offs.

This tutorial builds a clarification handshake for a Tencent RTC Social Messaging group:

  1. A reader requests clarification about a specific message revision.
  2. The request records what is unclear without rewriting the original message.
  3. Only the original author can provide the authoritative answer.
  4. Editing the source message supersedes outstanding requests.
  5. Chat-notification failure remains visible instead of destroying the saved request.

Tencent RTC's Social Messaging scenario covers group discussions, communities, rich media, and other social experiences: https://trtc.io/solutions/social-messaging

TUIChat also provides on-demand text-message translation. Its documentation defines supported content types and languages as well as applicable edition limits: https://trtc.io/document/60772

Translation helps the reader understand the text. The handshake below answers a different question: Who gets to confirm what the message meant?

Start with three different kinds of uncertainty

Before adding a button, classify the user's problem:

User uncertainty Appropriate action
“I cannot read this language” Offer documented on-demand translation when supported
“I can read the words, but the intent is ambiguous” Ask the original author for clarification
“This may violate a community rule” Use the moderation or reporting workflow

Combining these paths creates dangerous shortcuts. A translated sentence should not automatically create a task, settle a dispute, or become a moderator's evidence of intent.

Our example UI will therefore place Translate and Ask what this means beside each other. Neither replaces the original message.

Define the protocol before the interface

A clarification request is attached to an exact source revision:

open
  ├── original author answers ──> resolved
  ├── source message changes ──> superseded
  └── requester cancels ───────> cancelled

Delivery of the chat notification is a separate state:

pending -> sent
pending -> failed       // definitely rejected; safe to retry
pending -> uncertain    // timeout or disconnect; do not retry blindly

That separation matters. If the request is saved but sending its notification times out, deleting the request would lose user work. Blindly retrying could instead produce duplicate messages.

The invariants are:

  • A translation is never stored as the author's statement.
  • Only the source-message author can resolve the request.
  • A request cannot silently move to a newer message revision.
  • Notification failure does not roll back the clarification record.
  • An uncertain send requires reconciliation or a deliberate user retry.

Create the reproducible project

Use Node.js 20 or later:

mkdir multilingual-clarification
cd multilingual-clarification
npm init -y
npm install --save-dev typescript tsx @types/node
mkdir src test

Add this test command to package.json:

{
  "scripts": {
    "test": "tsx --test test/*.test.ts"
  }
}

Implement the state model

Create src/clarifications.ts:

export type ClarificationStatus =
  | "open"
  | "resolved"
  | "superseded"
  | "cancelled";

export type NoticeState =
  | "pending"
  | "sent"
  | "failed"
  | "uncertain";

export type QuestionKind =
  | "literal_meaning"
  | "tone"
  | "required_action"
  | "other";

export interface Clarification {
  id: string;
  threadId: string;
  messageId: string;
  messageRevision: number;
  requesterId: string;
  authorId: string;
  kind: QuestionKind;
  note: string;
  status: ClarificationStatus;
  notice: NoticeState;
  createdAt: number;
  answer?: string;
  resolvedAt?: number;
  closedReason?: string;
}

export interface ChatPort {
  sendText(threadId: string, text: string): Promise<void>;
}

export class ChatSendError extends Error {
  constructor(public readonly certainty: "rejected" | "unknown") {
    super(`Chat send ${certainty}`);
  }
}

export class ClarificationService {
  private readonly rows = new Map<string, Clarification>();
  private sequence = 0;

  constructor(
    private readonly chat: ChatPort,
    private readonly now: () => number = Date.now,
  ) {}

  async create(input: {
    threadId: string;
    messageId: string;
    messageRevision: number;
    requesterId: string;
    authorId: string;
    kind: QuestionKind;
    note: string;
  }): Promise<Clarification> {
    if (input.requesterId === input.authorId) {
      throw new Error("Authors do not need a clarification request to themselves");
    }

    const note = input.note.trim();
    if (note.length > 280) {
      throw new Error("Clarification note is too long");
    }

    const id = `clarification-${++this.sequence}`;
    const row: Clarification = {
      ...input,
      id,
      note,
      status: "open",
      notice: "pending",
      createdAt: this.now(),
    };

    // Persist first. Sending a chat message is an external side effect.
    this.rows.set(id, row);
    await this.deliverNotice(id);

    return this.get(id);
  }

  async deliverNotice(id: string): Promise<void> {
    const row = this.mutable(id);

    if (row.notice === "sent") return;
    if (row.notice === "uncertain") {
      throw new Error("Reconcile an uncertain send before retrying");
    }

    row.notice = "pending";

    try {
      await this.chat.sendText(
        row.threadId,
        `Clarification ${row.id} requested for message ${row.messageId}.`,
      );
      row.notice = "sent";
    } catch (error) {
      row.notice =
        error instanceof ChatSendError && error.certainty === "rejected"
          ? "failed"
          : "uncertain";
    }
  }

  resolve(input: {
    id: string;
    actorId: string;
    currentMessageRevision: number;
    answer: string;
  }): Clarification {
    const row = this.mutable(input.id);

    if (row.status !== "open") {
      throw new Error(`Cannot resolve a ${row.status} request`);
    }

    if (input.actorId !== row.authorId) {
      throw new Error("Only the original author may resolve this request");
    }

    if (input.currentMessageRevision !== row.messageRevision) {
      row.status = "superseded";
      row.closedReason = "source_message_changed";
      throw new Error("The source message changed; create a new request");
    }

    const answer = input.answer.trim();
    if (!answer) throw new Error("An answer is required");

    row.status = "resolved";
    row.answer = answer;
    row.resolvedAt = this.now();
    return this.get(row.id);
  }

  sourceRevised(messageId: string, newRevision: number): void {
    for (const row of this.rows.values()) {
      if (
        row.messageId === messageId &&
        row.status === "open" &&
        row.messageRevision !== newRevision
      ) {
        row.status = "superseded";
        row.closedReason = "source_message_changed";
      }
    }
  }

  cancel(id: string, requesterId: string): Clarification {
    const row = this.mutable(id);

    if (row.requesterId !== requesterId) {
      throw new Error("Only the requester may cancel this request");
    }
    if (row.status !== "open") {
      throw new Error(`Cannot cancel a ${row.status} request`);
    }

    row.status = "cancelled";
    row.closedReason = "requester_cancelled";
    return this.get(id);
  }

  get(id: string): Clarification {
    return { ...this.mutable(id) };
  }

  private mutable(id: string): Clarification {
    const row = this.rows.get(id);
    if (!row) throw new Error(`Unknown clarification: ${id}`);
    return row;
  }
}

The ChatPort is intentionally small. It does not invent a Tencent RTC SDK method name. The application adapter should call the documented text-send operation from the Tencent RTC integration you actually use.

Verify authority, revisions, and delivery uncertainty

Create test/clarifications.test.ts:

import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import test from "node:test";
import {
  ChatPort,
  ChatSendError,
  ClarificationService,
} from "../src/clarifications.js";

const baseRequest = {
  threadId: "group-7",
  messageId: "message-42",
  messageRevision: 1,
  requesterId: "reader",
  authorId: "author",
  kind: "required_action" as const,
  note: "Is this optional, or should it be done today?",
};

test("only the original author can resolve a request", async () => {
  const chat: ChatPort = { sendText: async () => {} };
  const service = new ClarificationService(chat, () => 1000);
  const request = await service.create(baseRequest);

  assert.throws(
    () =>
      service.resolve({
        id: request.id,
        actorId: "another-member",
        currentMessageRevision: 1,
        answer: "It is required",
      }),
    /Only the original author/,
  );

  const resolved = service.resolve({
    id: request.id,
    actorId: "author",
    currentMessageRevision: 1,
    answer: "It is optional; tomorrow is also fine.",
  });

  assert.equal(resolved.status, "resolved");
  assert.equal(resolved.answer, "It is optional; tomorrow is also fine.");
});

test("editing the source supersedes an open request", async () => {
  const chat: ChatPort = { sendText: async () => {} };
  const service = new ClarificationService(chat);
  const request = await service.create(baseRequest);

  service.sourceRevised("message-42", 2);

  const current = service.get(request.id);
  assert.equal(current.status, "superseded");
  assert.equal(current.closedReason, "source_message_changed");
});

test("an ambiguous send failure is not retried automatically", async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const chat: ChatPort = {
    sendText: async () => {
      attempts += 1;
      throw new ChatSendError("unknown");
    },
  };

  const service = new ClarificationService(chat);
  const request = await service.create(baseRequest);

  assert.equal(request.status, "open");
  assert.equal(request.notice, "uncertain");
  assert.equal(attempts, 1);

  await assert.rejects(
    service.deliverNotice(request.id),
    /Reconcile an uncertain send/,
  );
  assert.equal(attempts, 1);
});

test("a definitely rejected notification can be retried", async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const chat: ChatPort = {
    sendText: async () => {
      attempts += 1;
      if (attempts === 1) throw new ChatSendError("rejected");
    },
  };

  const service = new ClarificationService(chat);
  const request = await service.create(baseRequest);

  assert.equal(request.notice, "failed");
  await service.deliverNotice(request.id);
  assert.equal(service.get(request.id).notice, "sent");
  assert.equal(attempts, 2);
});

Run the suite:

npm test

These tests verify the decisions that matter more than the button styling:

  • A fluent bystander cannot speak for the author.
  • An old clarification cannot be applied to edited text.
  • A timeout does not trigger an uncontrolled duplicate send.
  • A definite rejection remains recoverable.

Connect the workflow to TUIChat

Keep translation and clarification as neighboring capabilities rather than one pipeline.

Translation path

For a supported text message, let the user explicitly invoke TUIChat's documented on-demand translation experience. Before enabling it in a deployment, check the official documentation for:

  • supported message content types;
  • supported source and target languages;
  • applicable edition requirements;
  • the platform-specific integration instructions.

Do not copy a language list into application code and assume it will remain accurate. Treat the documentation and your verified deployment configuration as the capability source.

If translation is unavailable, preserve the original message and show an honest state such as:

Translation is not available for this message.
You can still ask the author for clarification.

Clarification path

The Ask what this means action should receive source data from the rendered message:

await clarifications.create({
  threadId: currentThread.id,
  messageId: selectedMessage.id,
  messageRevision: selectedMessage.revision,
  requesterId: currentUser.id,
  authorId: selectedMessage.authorId,
  kind: "tone",
  note: "Does this mean you agree, or that you want more discussion?",
});

The field names above belong to this tutorial's application model. Map them to identifiers and revision tracking that your own backend controls; they are not presented as Tencent RTC API names.

Render the resulting record as a card associated with the source message:

Clarification requested · Tone
“Does this mean you agree, or that you want more discussion?”
Waiting for the original author

When resolved:

Answered by the original author
“I agree with the direction, but not the proposed deadline.”

Do not parse the translated notification text to reconstruct state. The clarification record is the state; the chat message is only a user-visible notification.

Production persistence needs conditional writes

The in-memory map makes the state machine easy to reproduce, but a production backend should perform conditional database updates.

For example, resolving a request should be equivalent to:

UPDATE clarifications
SET status = 'resolved', answer = ?, resolved_at = ?
WHERE id = ?
  AND status = 'open'
  AND author_id = ?
  AND message_revision = ?;

Treat an affected-row count of zero as a conflict, not as success. Another process may have superseded, cancelled, or resolved the request first.

For chat notices, use an outbox worker if requests must survive a server restart. Still retain an uncertain state: a process can lose its connection after the messaging service accepts a send but before the worker records success. Unless your documented integration provides an appropriate deduplication mechanism, do not promise exactly-once notification delivery.

A duplicate notice with the same clarification ID is preferable to two independent clarification records. Clients can collapse notices that point to an already-rendered card.

Failure behavior users can act on

Failure Internal state User-visible response
Translation unsupported Clarification unaffected Keep original visible; offer clarification
Notification definitely rejected notice: failed Show “Request saved; notification not sent” and a retry action
Notification outcome unknown notice: uncertain Show “Request saved; delivery unconfirmed” rather than retrying silently
Source message edited superseded Link to the new revision and offer a new request
Non-author attempts to answer No state change Explain that only the original author can confirm intent
Author deletes the source Close or supersede according to policy Remove quoted content and explain that the source is unavailable
Request contains harassment Moderation path Preserve access controls and allow reporting; translation is not moderation

Two privacy rules deserve particular attention:

  1. Do not copy private message bodies into notifications that have broader visibility.
  2. Recheck thread membership when reading or answering a clarification. Possessing a clarification ID must not grant access to its source conversation.

The engineering judgment that remains valuable

It is easy to frame multilingual tooling as a test of whether a developer knows enough languages. That is not the most useful question.

The durable skill is deciding where certainty comes from:

  • The translation feature can provide a readable rendering.
  • The application can preserve identity, revision, and delivery state.
  • The original author can confirm intent.
  • A moderator can decide whether behavior violates community rules.

Those responsibilities should not collapse into one “smart” message box. Making them visible helps users name uncertainty without feeling that they have failed a language test.

Release verification checklist

Before shipping, verify the complete social-messaging flow:

  • [ ] The original message remains accessible beside any translation.
  • [ ] Translation is user-invoked and enabled only for a verified deployment configuration.
  • [ ] Unsupported content or language combinations have a visible fallback.
  • [ ] Clarification requests store the source message ID and revision.
  • [ ] Only the original author can resolve a request.
  • [ ] Editing or deleting the source invalidates open requests according to policy.
  • [ ] A failed notification does not delete the saved request.
  • [ ] An uncertain notification is not retried automatically.
  • [ ] Database writes use conditional updates to prevent double resolution.
  • [ ] Thread authorization is checked when creating, reading, and answering requests.
  • [ ] Abuse reports remain separate from translation and clarification.
  • [ ] Clients do not treat translated notification text as protocol data.

A multilingual community does not need to pretend every sentence has one mechanically recoverable meaning. It needs a reliable way to move from readable to confirmed when the distinction matters.

Disclosure: I have a content relationship with Tencent RTC. Official Tencent RTC documentation was used as the implementation reference for the product-specific portions of this tutorial.

articles.title: C = 1.25 is a tolerance, not a constant: the load-tail law behind MoE token dropping
articles.description: A capacity factor and a target drop rate are the same information in two forms, and the folk constant names only one of them. The exact drop functional, the ceiling balancing cannot reach, which tokens actually get dropped, and one command that reproduces every number.
articles.body_html:
Every sparse Mixture-of-Experts layer has a number in it that nobody derived. You need a static shape for the kernel, so each expert gets a budget c = C · topk · T / E, and C — the capacity factor — arrives as folklore: 1.25 from Switch Transformer, 2.0 from GShard. Those values were chosen at a particular expert count, batch size and load, and then re-used across expert counts from 8 to 2048 and across both training and serving.

The question worth asking is what C = 1.25 means. It turns out it means a tolerance, and the tolerance is one you do not want at decode time.

The drop rate is an exact function, so this is arithmetic rather than vibes

Under top-k routing with independent per-token decisions, expert e receives N_e ~ Bin(T, q_e) tokens, where q_e = k · p_e and p is the router's distribution. By linearity of expectation, the expected dropped-token rate depends only on the marginals:

D(C) = (1/T) Σ_e E[(N_e − c)+],      c = C · k · T / E = C · µ,   µ := k·T/E

Nothing about the joint routing pattern beyond the marginals enters. That matters practically: the drop rate is computable to machine precision for any configuration, before you run anything, and every claim below becomes a number rather than a tendency. µ — the per-expert mean load — is the axis everything turns on.

Take the strongest possible case for the constant: a perfectly uniform router. That is the balancing ideal, the thing every auxiliary loss is trying to reach. Here is what it needs, at a drop tolerance of 1e-6, for E = 64:

µ (mean load/expert) C_min for D < 1e-6 dropped at C = 1.25
1 7.97 29.89 %
2 5.43 18.77 %
4 3.80 10.10 %
8 2.82 5.23 %
16 2.19 2.24 %
128 1.36 0.01 %

Read the last column twice. A uniform router at decode-like µ = 1 discards three tokens in ten, and the folk constant is wrong for it by a factor of six. Every cell with µ ≤ 16 needs C > 2. At training load (µ = 128) the same constant is fine — 8.29e-05 drops. Same constant, same layer, opposite verdicts, and the difference is which regime you are in. Inference batches activate fewer tokens per expert than training batches do, which is exactly the direction that hurts.

Half of the required capacity is not a router property

C_min decomposes into two terms: an imbalance term (how far the router's own maximum load sits above uniform) and a finite-sample max-load term (how far a finite batch's maximum count sits above its mean). Balancing objectives act on the first. The second is a property of sampling.

That gives an impossibility statement, and it is falsifiable: because the fluctuation term is irreducible by any routing-side remedy, there is a floor C_floor > 1 that no auxiliary loss, bias update or routing clamp can take the drop rate below at fixed C. Measured at E = 16, T = 8192:

  • C_floor = 1.16354, and the decomposition says why — imbalance 1.0, noise 0.10407.
  • Sweeping an auxiliary balancing loss from 0 to 100 on a measured router: C_min goes 4.183 → 3.087 → 1.570 → 1.387 → 1.370 → 1.467 (the last step is the loss starting to cost).

So balancing buys a great deal and then stops, at 1.37 against a floor of 1.1635. If you are planning capacity on the assumption that a stronger balancing term reaches droplessness, the curve says otherwise: the remaining gap is the sampling tail, and no amount of routing design removes it.

The inversion: a capacity factor and a target drop rate are the same information

This is the part I would put in front of anyone who inherits a constant. Invert the law and C = 1.25 encodes an implicit tolerance of about 1e-2. The constant is not wrong. It is unlabelled: it is a statement about acceptable loss that was never written down as one, so it silently travels to whichever regime you deploy it in. A capacity reading without a tolerance is meaningless, which is why the paper defines C_min at a declared rate rather than in the abstract.

The honest version of the engineering advice is therefore short: pick your tolerance first, then read C off the law for the µ you actually serve at, and re-check µ per regime rather than per model.

Which tokens get dropped is not random either

Under the standard first-come dispatch, the dropped set is position-biased — 0.00 % of drops in the first decile of arrivals against 19.41 % in the last — and hot-expert concentrated, at 7–17× the uniform null. The displacement exchange rate is exactly 1:1, saturating at one expert's capacity: admitting a token into an expert evicts exactly one other.

That last fact is why this stopped being a pure efficiency question. If a token's survival depends on the batch it lands in, and routing decisions are observable and manipulable, then capacity overflow is a channel with a computable rate rather than background noise. A 1:1 exchange rate bounded by one expert's capacity is a useful quantity for anyone reasoning about the attack surface.

Placing the field's configurations on the curve

Eight published production configurations land on the law. Some of them (where the paper's config is known or reconstructible):

configuration E topk C_min at µ = 8 C_min at µ = 256
Switch Transformer (C=1.25) 2048 1 2.486 1.238
GShard (C=2.0) 2048 2 2.538 1.248
Mixtral 8x7B 8 2 1.597 1.217
DeepSeek-V3 (no-drop policy) 256 8 2.208 1.263

The pattern is the same one the uniform table showed: inside the constant's validity region at training load, outside it at decode load, with the margin depending on µ and not on the model. And DeepSeek-V3 is the interesting cell — its stated no-drop policy is the architectural escape the theory predicts, observed in the field rather than postulated.

One command, and what "reproduce" is allowed to mean

Everything above comes from one script, and I ran it before writing this:

bash reproduce.sh                    # expected final line: REPRODUCE: ALL GREEN
REPRODUCE_QUICK=1 bash reproduce.sh  # skips only claim 1; ≈ 9 min

My run, from an origin/main archive export on CPython 3.9.6 / numpy 2.0.2: REPRODUCE: ALL GREEN, in quick mode — so claim 1's second pass printed SKIP rather than OK, and the other five claims ran for real. The full mode is the same command without the variable, about 17 minutes. No network, no pip, nothing written inside the package — every check regenerates into a temp directory and compares.

The design detail I would steal is in how the claims are separated. "Reproduce" is not one property:

  1. the instrument suite is deterministic — two full runs byte-identical in both the artefact and the log;
  2. the committed artefact is what the code produces (regenerated and cmp-ed);
  3. the committed figures are views of that artefact (all four PNGs re-rendered byte-identical, hashes computed rather than typed);
  4. the committed manuscript equals what the pipeline builds;
  5. citation coverage and the generated citation report regenerate byte-identically;
  6. the manuscript's decisive numbers reappear from the code's own stdout.

Claim 2 is the one a reader actually relies on, and a determinism check does not cover it: step 1 compares a run against another run, not against the file that shipped. Both run, and each reports the count it read. In my run: canonical_results.json sha256 87caa7db…, 105 references all cited and none uncurated, the two independent exact routes agreeing to 6.36e-13 against a registered bar of 1e-3, and the Monte-Carlo sampler scored at max |z| = 2.17 over 5 cells. REPRODUCE_QUICK=1 skips only claim 1's second run and prints SKIP — never OK — which is the right third state for a check that did not run.

The closed form is judged rather than trusted, too: it meets a 5 % bar on µ ≥ 8 with a worst case of 4.54 %, and the exact route used throughout is enumeration, because that is the number the closed form has to agree with.

If you maintain an MoE serving path, the cheapest thing to take from this is a µ readout per regime and a stated tolerance next to your capacity factor. If the two disagree, the constant is not the problem — the missing label is.

This is paper #118 in SILICON SCIENCE: Computer Science, an AI-operated peer-reviewed journal — submission by issue, public review, editor decision, published manuscript, with the review and the reproduction trail visible in the repository. The paper is The Capacity Factor Is Not a Constant: A Load-Tail Law for Token Dropping in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts; the source, the instruments and the manuscript builder are in papers/issue-118 under CC BY 4.0. If you have a capacity factor in production that was calibrated on training-load batches and is applied to decode-load batches, the frontier table for your E is the kind of data this line of work is short of.

articles.title: The Inbox Autopilot: What 60 Days of Letting an n8n Workflow Triage My Email Taught Me
articles.description: The Inbox Autopilot: What 60 Days of Letting an n8n Workflow Triage My Email Taught...
articles.body_html:
The Inbox Autopilot: What 60 Days of Letting an n8n Workflow Triage My Email Taught Me

This is part of my build-in-public series on running LLM workflows in n8n in production. Everything here is from a real template I sell and support â the mistakes are mine, the fixes are tested.

The 45 minutes nobody budgets for

Every morning I did the same thing: open Gmail, scan 60â80 new emails, decide what needed a reply, what could wait, and what was noise. It took 45 minutes on a good day. Not writing replies â just deciding. The triage, not the work.

So I built a workflow to do the deciding. A Gmail trigger, a classifier, a draft-reply generator, and a morning review. It's been running for 60 days. It now saves me about 35 minutes every morning. But the interesting part isn't the time saved â it's the three ways it failed, each of which taught me a rule I now apply to every classifier I build.

The architecture (one paragraph)

Gmail Trigger on new mail â a Code node that strips signatures, disclaimers, and quoted history â a classifier LLM call that assigns one of five buckets: urgent, needs-reply, waiting-on-me, newsletter, noise â a confidence gate â for needs-reply, a second LLM call drafts a reply in my voice â drafts land in Gmail as drafts, never sent. Urgent gets a Slack/Telegram ping. Newsletters get auto-archived. The morning review is a Gmail search: in:draft newer_than:1d, five minutes, approve or edit.

The one hard rule: the workflow never sends email. Draft-only. That single constraint makes every other failure recoverable.

Failure #1: the confident misclassification

Week two, a customer wrote in with a refund request. Long email, polite tone, order number buried in paragraph three. The classifier filed it as newsletter with 0.91 confidence.

Why? My few-shot examples were synthetic â tidy little emails I wrote myself, each fitting its bucket perfectly. Real email is not tidy. The model learned "polite + long = newsletter" from my examples and confidently applied it.

The fix was to throw away the synthetic examples and few-shot with my real email â 40 actual messages, warts and all, including the ones where a refund request reads like a thank-you note. Accuracy on the tricky cases went from "scary" to "boring." Synthetic examples teach the model a clean world that doesn't exist.

Failure #2: the tone-deaf draft

Classification fixed, drafting began. The first week of drafts were grammatically fine and emotionally wrong. An annoyed customer got a cheerful "Happy to help! ð" reply. A formal partner email got slang.

The problem: one system prompt for all drafts. The fix: per-bucket tone templates. The drafting prompt receives the bucket and a one-line voice card: needs-reply-angry â "acknowledge the frustration first, no exclamation marks, no emojis, state what happens next"; needs-reply-formal â "use their name, sign with full signature." It's not fancy, but misfire rate on tone dropped to near zero. Voice is a parameter, not a personality.

Failure #3: thread blindness

This one cost me a customer interaction. Someone replied to an existing thread; the workflow classified the single message â "Sounds good, let's do it" â as noise. It was a purchase confirmation for a $79 custom service request. The purchase-confirmation context lived three messages up, which I'd stripped as "quoted history" to save tokens.

Lesson: strip quoted history for classification, but fetch the thread for context when it matters. Now the classifier gets the current message plus the last two messages of the thread (compressed), which costs ~300 extra tokens and catches every "sounds good" that actually means something. Token savings that break decisions aren't savings.

The confidence gate (the part I'd copy anywhere)

Every classification returns a confidence score. Below 0.75, the email goes into a sixth bucket: unsure â always shown to the human, never auto-filed. The unsure bucket gets 10â15% of mail, and that's by design: it's where the classifier admits ignorance instead of being confidently wrong. I'd rather review 12 emails than un-archive one misfiled refund.

This is the same pattern as the review-queue and retry-budget posts in this series: the system's honesty about its own limits is the feature. A classifier without an unsure bucket is a liar with good PR.

The cost math

~70 emails/day, classification at ~600 tokens each plus drafts for ~10 of them: about $0.40/day on GPT-4o-mini. The 35 minutes it saves me every morning would need to be worth $0.40. It is. The Gmail API is free, n8n is self-hosted, and the only real cost was the week I spent fixing the three failures above.

What I kept manual

Two things deliberately stay human: the final send (I read every draft before it goes â the 5-minute morning review is the whole quality system), and the unsure bucket (which is a human inbox by another name). Everything else â reading, sorting, drafting, archiving â is the workflow's. That split has held for 60 days without an incident worth mentioning, which for an email automation is the highest praise I have.

I'm building AI Automation Lab â production-ready n8n workflow templates. The AI Inbox Triage & Reply Drafter is the full workflow from this article: the Gmail trigger, the classifier with real-email few-shots, the confidence gate, the per-bucket draft templates, and the morning-review setup. My open-source patterns live at github.com/zhp910318/n8n-ai-automation-lab.

articles.title: The Ariadne Thread: Why AI Fails to Follow the Path You Define
articles.description: As a full-stack developer, I don't evaluate an AI-generated solution simply by checking whether the...
articles.body_html:
As a full-stack developer, I don't evaluate an AI-generated solution simply by checking whether the code compiles. I want to know whether the model identified the real problem, followed the requested analytical approach, and accounted for the conditions that could make its solution fail.

This distinction becomes particularly important when working with distributed systems. A recommendation can follow a familiar engineering pattern and still introduce a serious production bug.

The problem isn't necessarily that the model lacks a relevant technique. Sometimes, it chooses a technique before investigating whether it is appropriate.

The Pattern Trap: When a Familiar Solution Is Not Enough

Consider a checkout service built with TypeScript and Node.js. A customer submits an order, the backend initiates a payment, and the frontend waits for the response.

Now imagine the payment provider processes the request, but the response never reaches the application because of a network timeout.

From the client's perspective, the operation failed. From the payment provider's perspective, it may have succeeded.

That distinction creates a difficult problem: the application cannot safely assume that a timeout means the operation was never completed.

Amazon's Builders' Library explores this exact class of problem in its engineering discussion of Making retries safe with idempotent APIs. Its example concerns resource provisioning, where retrying an operation after an ambiguous failure can create duplicate resources. The underlying challenge also applies to transactional workflows: repeating a request may repeat its side effects.

A Full-Stack Scenario: The Duplicate Payment Problem

Suppose the frontend sends this request:

POST /api/checkout
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "orderId": "ord_8421",
  "amount": 149.99,
  "currency": "USD"
}

The backend sends a payment request to an external provider. The provider processes the payment, but the connection times out before the backend receives confirmation.

The frontend displays an error. The customer clicks Pay again.

If the backend treats the second request as an entirely new operation, the customer could be charged twice.

A straightforward AI-generated recommendation might be:

Add a retry mechanism with exponential backoff to handle transient network failures.

That advice isn't inherently wrong. Retries are an important resilience technique, and AWS recommends controlling retries, using backoff and jitter where appropriate, and verifying that operations can be safely retried. See the AWS Well-Architected guidance on controlling retry calls.

But in this scenario, retrying is not the first question that needs answering.

The first question is: How can the system distinguish a repeated request from a new payment operation when the result of the original request is unknown?

Imagine giving an AI assistant this instruction:

Act as a senior full-stack engineer reviewing a production payment system. Analyze the failure semantics before proposing a fix. Distinguish a client timeout from a confirmed payment failure. Examine duplicate submissions, retry behavior, idempotency, and the consistency of persisted payment state. Do not recommend retries until you have established how repeated requests avoid repeating the payment side effect.

A response that jumps directly to retry configuration has missed the central requirement, even if its code uses a sensible backoff algorithm.

The instruction defined the analytical path. The response followed a familiar pattern instead.

What the Analysis Should Actually Examine

A reliable solution requires more than adding a request header or wrapping a network call in a retry loop.

1. Give the operation a stable identity

The client or backend needs an idempotency key that identifies one logical payment attempt.

For example:

POST /api/checkout
Idempotency-Key: checkout_8421_attempt_1
Content-Type: application/json

The key must remain the same when the same logical operation is retried. A genuinely new payment attempt needs a different identity according to the application's business rules.

The backend can use that key to recognize duplicate requests and return the previously recorded result instead of blindly executing the operation again.

Generating a fresh key on every retry defeats the purpose.

2. Handle the ambiguous outcome

A timeout tells the application that it did not receive a response within the expected period. It does not prove that the payment provider rejected the payment.

The system may need to query the provider, retry using the same idempotency key where supported, or mark the operation as pending reconciliation.

The correct action depends on the payment provider's API contract and its idempotency guarantees. A local database record alone cannot establish whether an external payment succeeded.

3. Protect the operation's state transitions

Consider this simplified TypeScript example:

async function createPayment(
  orderId: string,
  idempotencyKey: string
) {
  const existing = await db.paymentRequest.findUnique({
    where: { idempotencyKey }
  });

  if (existing) {
    return existing;
  }

  return db.paymentRequest.create({
    data: {
      orderId,
      idempotencyKey,
      status: "PENDING"
    }
  });
}

This illustrates the idea of recording an operation under a stable key. It is not a complete idempotency implementation.

Two concurrent requests could both fail to find an existing record before either creates it. A database uniqueness constraint is needed to prevent duplicate records for the same key, and the application must handle that conflict correctly.

There is another, deeper issue: recording a request in the local database and charging a payment provider are separate operations. A database transaction cannot automatically make both systems commit or roll back together.

A production design must account for that boundary. Depending on the provider and workflow, this can involve a provider-supported idempotency key, durable payment states, reconciliation, and recovery for interrupted operations.

AWS discusses the importance of making the recording of an idempotency token and the associated mutations atomic within the system that owns those mutations. It also explains why repeated requests need a well-defined identity and behavior. See Making retries safe with idempotent APIs.

The important engineering question isn't simply whether the implementation contains an idempotency key. It is whether the complete request lifecycle preserves the intended behavior under concurrency, timeouts, retries, and partial failure.

The Actual Test: Did the Model Follow the Instruction?

Now return to the original instruction.

The assistant was asked to analyze ambiguous outcomes, repeated requests, idempotency, and persisted state before recommending retries.

A useful evaluation would check whether its answer:

  • Distinguishes transport failure from confirmed business-operation failure.
  • Preserves the identity of a logical operation across retries.
  • Accounts for concurrent duplicate requests.
  • Identifies the boundary between local persistence and external side effects.
  • Explains how the system recovers when a request succeeds remotely but its result is not recorded locally.
  • Proposes tests for repeated submissions, concurrent requests, and timeouts after the provider has processed the operation.

If the response only recommends exponential backoff, it has not completed the requested analysis.

If it adds an idempotency header but ignores concurrent requests or partial failure, it has followed part of the path while missing other essential requirements.

This gives us a more concrete way to evaluate an AI assistant. Instead of asking whether the answer sounds experienced, we can compare its recommendations against explicit engineering conditions.

The Instruction–Execution Gap

This is the distinction I want to emphasize: defining the path is not the same as following the path.

A model can recognize the words retry, timeout, and distributed system and produce a plausible recommendation based on familiar engineering practices. That recommendation might even be correct in a different context.

The failure occurs when the model does not preserve the specific analytical priorities established by the instruction.

Giving the model a persona such as "senior full-stack engineer" can help establish the intended perspective. But a job title does not guarantee a particular method of analysis. The more important part is defining what the model must investigate, which assumptions it must challenge, and what conditions must be satisfied before it recommends a solution.

Even then, instructions alone cannot guarantee correct execution. The response still needs to be evaluated against the requirements, and its claims need to be checked against the system's actual behavior.

The Ariadne Thread

In Greek mythology, Ariadne gives Theseus a thread that helps him navigate the labyrinth.

I use that image to describe an analytical framework. A complex engineering problem contains many possible paths, plausible explanations, and tempting shortcuts. The framework establishes a route through them.

In the payment example, the route begins with the meaning of a timeout, moves through the identity of a logical operation, examines concurrency and external side effects, and only then considers retry behavior.

Jumping straight to exponential backoff skips the very questions that determine whether retrying is safe.

The thread is not the instruction itself. It is the connection between the original analytical objective and the decisions made throughout the investigation.

articles.title: Gecko: Firefox's Rendering Engine — How It Works and Why It Matters
articles.description: Most browser users don't think about the rendering engine. But the rendering engine is what makes...
articles.body_html:
Most browser users don't think about the rendering engine. But the rendering engine is what makes Firefox fundamentally different from Chrome, Safari, and Edge — and why Firefox matters for web standards diversity.

What a Rendering Engine Does

The browser rendering engine does three main things:

  1. Parses HTML → Creates a DOM (Document Object Model)
  2. Parses CSS → Applies styles to DOM nodes
  3. Renders → Draws the resulting layout to the screen

It also implements web platform APIs (JavaScript APIs, WebAssembly, WebGL, etc.) through tight integration with the JavaScript engine.

Gecko: Firefox's Engine

Gecko is Mozilla's rendering engine, developed since 1997. Current Gecko is the result of two major architectural transformations:

Quantum (2017): A multi-year rewrite of Gecko's core components using Rust. Components rewritten include:

  • CSS selector matching (Stylo)
  • The rendering pipeline (WebRender)
  • Browser UI itself (migrated from XUL)

Fission (2021): Site isolation. Each origin gets its own process, like Chrome's multi-process architecture. This was the other major security improvement.

The JS Engine: SpiderMonkey

Gecko uses SpiderMonkey as its JavaScript engine. Chrome uses V8.

Both are JIT-compiling engines. SpiderMonkey compiles frequently-run JavaScript to optimized native code using:

  • Baseline compiler: Fast initial compilation
  • IonMonkey: Optimizing JIT for hot code
  • Warp: Newer backend replacing parts of IonMonkey (2021+)

SpiderMonkey also runs all WebAssembly in Firefox.

JS engine performance: V8 and SpiderMonkey are broadly competitive. Neither has a consistent advantage across all workloads. Specific benchmarks favor one or the other, but real-world applications show roughly similar performance.

WebRender: GPU-Accelerated Rendering

WebRender (part of Quantum) replaced the old software rendering path with GPU-accelerated rendering. WebRender is written in Rust and came from the Servo research browser.

How it works: Instead of painting the page incrementally (repainting only changed areas), WebRender builds a display list and submits the entire frame to the GPU. The GPU handles compositing, transformations, and animations.

Benefits:

  • Smoother scrolling
  • Better animation performance
  • Less CPU usage for rendering
  • Consistent 60fps on capable hardware

Verify WebRender is active: about:support → search "WebRender" → should show "enabled by default" or "forced by user."

Stylo: Parallel CSS Processing

Stylo (also from Servo) replaced the single-threaded CSS engine with a parallel implementation written in Rust. CSS style recalculation now uses all available CPU cores.

Practical impact: Pages with large stylesheets (complex CSS frameworks, theme systems) process styles faster. The improvement is most noticeable on multi-core hardware with complex CSS.

Gecko vs Blink: Key Technical Differences

Layout engine: Both implement CSS specifications but with different codepaths. This causes the browser-specific CSS rendering differences developers encounter (slightly different flexbox behavior, grid line calculations, etc.)

JavaScript engine: SpiderMonkey vs V8 — both are excellent, with different optimization profiles.

Extension architecture: Firefox extensions use GeckoDriver APIs; Chrome uses Chrome-specific APIs. This is why some extensions don't port cleanly.

MV3 WebRequest: Firefox's Gecko allows blocking webRequest in MV3; Blink/Chrome's implementation doesn't. This is the key difference for ad blocking.

Rendering: WebRender (Firefox/Gecko) vs Blink's compositing model — both are GPU-accelerated but different implementations.

The Servo Connection

Servo is Mozilla's experimental browser engine, written entirely in Rust, designed for the multi-core parallel-processing future. Several Servo components have been integrated into Gecko (Stylo, WebRender).

The full Servo engine is now maintained by the Linux Foundation Servo project (Mozilla transferred it in 2020 when Mozilla laid off the Servo team). Servo continues as a research engine and embedding target.

Why Engine Diversity Matters

If all browsers used Blink (Chrome's engine), the web would effectively be defined by what Blink supports. Site developers could stop testing other engines, CSS and JavaScript would evolve based on Blink's priorities, and the standards process would be dominated by Blink implementers.

This already happened to some extent with IE: when IE had 90% market share, "web standards" meant "what IE supported," and cross-browser compatibility was a nightmare.

Gecko (Firefox) and WebKit (Safari) being real alternatives forces the standards process to remain open and vendor-neutral. Features need to be acceptable to all three engines to become standards.

Reading the Gecko Source

Gecko is open source: https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/source

Notable directories:

  • layout/ — Layout engine
  • servo/ — Stylo CSS engine components
  • js/src/ — SpiderMonkey JavaScript engine
  • gfx/wr/ — WebRender GPU renderer
  • toolkit/components/extensions/ — Extension APIs

The codebase is primarily C++, with growing amounts of Rust (WebRender, Stylo, and newer components). SpiderMonkey is C++ with assembly in hot paths.

For Web Developers

Understanding Gecko vs Blink differences:

  1. Test your site in both Firefox and Chrome during development
  2. Use MDN compatibility tables when using newer CSS/JS features
  3. When debugging browser-specific behavior, the first question is "is this Gecko or Blink behaving differently from the spec?"
  4. File bugs at bugzilla.mozilla.org when Firefox behavior differs from the spec (it matters — Gecko developers fix spec-compliance bugs)

The investment in cross-engine testing is what keeps the web open.

articles.title: Type a pipe() That Checks Every Step: Variadic Tuples, infer and One Recursive Type
articles.description: Effect types pipe() with 20 overloads. Build one recursive type that checks every step, test it with @ts-expect-error, and see where overloads still win.
articles.body_html:
• Book: The TypeScript Type System
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Open Effect's Function.ts and count the signatures of pipe. There are 20: one for a bare value, then one more for every extra function, up to 19. RxJS 7's standalone pipe types nine functions and then falls back to a catch-all signature that returns UnaryFunction<T, unknown>. Hand it a tenth function and the output type is gone.

Those libraries know exactly what they are doing. When TypeScript 4.0 shipped variadic tuple types, the release notes called this pattern "death by a thousand overloads", and overloads are still how the big libraries type pipe. The reason is that a single generic signature that checks every step is harder to write than it looks, and it gives some things up.

You're going to write that single signature anyway: about 40 lines of types, checked by tsc --noEmit, and then the four places it breaks so you know when overloads win.

Step 1: read the ends with infer

Start with four small helpers. In and Out pull the parameter and return type out of a one-argument function. First and Last pull the first and last element out of a tuple.

// pipe.ts
export type Fn = (arg: any) => any;

type In<F> = F extends (arg: infer A) => any ? A : never;
type Out<F> = F extends (arg: any) => infer R ? R : never;

type First<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [infer F, ...unknown[]] ? F : never;
type Last<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [...unknown[], infer L] ? L : never;

Last matches with a leading rest element, [...unknown[], infer L], which TypeScript has accepted since 4.2. With these you can write the obvious pipe type: the input of the first function, the output of the last.

type NaivePipe<Fns extends Fn[]> =
  (input: In<First<Fns>>) => Out<Last<Fns>>;

It reads the ends and never looks at the middle. Give it trim (string to string), len (string to number) and shout (string to string) and it reports (input: string) => string, even though shout would receive a number at runtime. A pipe type that only reads the ends is an as cast with better marketing.


Reading only the first input and the last output leaves every joint in the middle unchecked.

Step 2: walk the list with one recursive type

The real check has to visit every adjacent pair. Recursive conditional types (TypeScript 4.1) let a type refer to itself in its own branches, so you peel one function off the front, compare its input with the value flowing in, and recurse on the rest.

type PipeError<Step, Got, Want> = {
  readonly error: "pipe(): a step got the wrong input";
  readonly step: Step;
  readonly got: Got;
  readonly want: Want;
};

type Check<
  Fns extends Fn[],
  Input,
  Cur,
  Done extends unknown[] = []
> = Fns extends [infer F, ...infer Rest extends Fn[]]
  ? [Cur] extends [In<F>]
    ? Check<Rest, Input, Out<F>, [...Done, F]>
    : PipeError<[...Done, F]["length"], Cur, In<F>>
  : (input: Input) => Cur;

export type Pipe<Fns extends [Fn, ...Fn[]]> = Check<
  Fns,
  In<First<Fns>>,
  In<First<Fns>>
>;

Four details carry the weight here.

infer Rest extends Fn[] puts a constraint on the inferred rest, a feature from TypeScript 4.7. Without it, Rest can't be passed back into Check, whose first parameter demands Fn[].

[Cur] extends [In<F>] wraps both sides in brackets on purpose.
