Evaluating only the final answer Misses bad trajectories, policy violations, and wasted steps Grade trajectory, outcome state, safety, cost, and latency (Section 11)
No adversarial tests Injection and exfiltration vulnerabilities ship undetected Continuous red-team suite as a release gate (Sections 10, 11)
Granting autonomy before earning it Failures happen at machine speed, unattended Start low on the autonomy ladder; promote with evidence (Section 6)
No audit trail or traces Incidents can't be investigated or debugged Trace every run; log decisions and approvals; protect the logs (Sections 8, 10)

Quick Reference Table

Concept Key idea Practical takeaway
Agent Model + control loop + tools + guardrails, pursuing a goal The model proposes; your code executes and enforces
Agent loop Think → act (tool) → observe → repeat Always bound it: steps, tokens, time, cost
Tool calling Model requests an external action (functions + hosted tools + MCP) Tool design is the highest-leverage work
Function calling Structured call matching a JSON schema Validate arguments; return helpful errors
Tool design Clear names/descriptions, right granularity, small results Few focused tools per agent; read/write separation
Planning Decide steps (implicit, or explicit plan-validate-execute) Fewer steps; verify along the way; replan on failure
Reliability math Per-step errors compound 95% × 10 steps ≈ 60% end-to-end
Working memory The context window for this run Compact; keep a scratchpad; trim tool output
Long-term memory Durable facts, episodes, procedures Provenance, per-user scoping, expiry, user control
Memory poisoning Planted false facts persist Don't auto-save from untrusted content
Autonomy levels Assistive → suggest → approve → bounded → supervised → full Start low; earn autonomy with evidence
Multi-agent Specialists coordinated by a supervisor/pipeline/router Start with one agent; add more only when measured
Orchestration Deterministic control flow around probabilistic steps Durable state, idempotent steps, timeouts, tracing
Human-in-the-loop Approval, clarification, escalation, audit Interrupt-and-resume; show the real action; authorize approvers
Prompt injection Untrusted text steers the model (direct/indirect) Assume it can succeed; limit what it can do
Lethal trifecta Private data + untrusted content + outbound communication Break at least one leg
Least privilege Minimum tools, per-user delegated credentials The cure for confused-deputy and excessive agency
Sandboxing Isolated, no-secret, limited-egress execution Never run model-generated code in your app process
Evaluation Outcome + trajectory + safety + cost + reliability Simulated environment, repeated runs, pass^k
Red-teaming Adversarial test suite (injection, exfiltration, privilege) Make it a release gate

Conclusion

An agent is a model, a control loop, a set of tools, and — most importantly — the guardrails and operational discipline around them. The model supplies judgment and flexibility; everything else is ordinary engineering that you can make deterministic, bounded, observable, and testable: budgets on every loop, a policy engine that decides in code which tool calls are allowed, denied, or sent to a human, durable state that survives restarts and approvals, and traces that make every decision auditable. The craft lies in tool design (clear, focused, least-privilege tools with helpful errors), in keeping the context lean, and in choosing the simplest architecture that works — a single call, then a workflow, then a bounded agent, and a multi-agent system only when measurement shows a single agent genuinely falls short.

Two themes decide whether an agent is trustworthy. The first is security by architecture: because no one can currently make a model perfectly distinguish instructions from data, assume prompt injection will sometimes succeed and design so that a hijacked agent cannot do serious harm — least privilege and per-user delegated credentials, no combination of private data, untrusted content, and outbound communication without a human gate, sandboxed execution, egress control, a vetted tool supply chain, and strict separation of what the model proposes from what your code permits. The second is evidence before autonomy: agents are non-deterministic and errors compound across steps, so you measure outcomes against real end state, grade trajectories and safety as well as answers, run every case many times and hold yourself to the strict all-runs-pass standard, attack your own agent with a red-team suite on every release, and grant independence one rung at a time as the numbers earn it. Build that way, and agents become a dependable way to automate open-ended work; skip it, and you have simply built a faster way to make mistakes.

Found this useful? Feel free to star the repo, open an issue with corrections, or share the "the agent obeyed instructions hidden in a support ticket" story that made the case for least privilege and human approval click better than any threat model.

articles.title: Your First Claude Code Mod: Block Edits Outside the Task's Worktree in 30 Lines
articles.description: Claude Code mods run your JavaScript on every tool call. Build a 30-line mod that refuses Edit and Write outside the task's worktree, then test it.
articles.body_html:
• Book: TypeScript Essentials
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Your agent is working in a git worktree, on its own branch, in a folder next to your main checkout. Then a stack trace from your dev server lands in its context. Every path in that trace points at the main checkout, one directory over. The agent opens ../app/src/config.ts, fixes the bug there, and your "isolated" task has just edited the copy you were using.

Worktrees keep agents apart on disk. They don't stop an agent from writing to a path outside its own folder. In Claude Code's acceptEdits mode, edits outside the working directory still ask you first, but bypassPermissions skips the prompts, and a prompt you approve at the end of a long day is still an approval.

Claude Code v2.1.287 and later can run mods: plugins whose JavaScript or TypeScript handlers run inside Claude Code when an event fires, such as a tool call. A handler can watch the event, change it, or answer it in Claude Code's place. This post builds one that answers Edit and Write calls aimed outside the session's folder with a refusal. It is 30 lines of JavaScript, plus two small JSON files.

What a mod is

A mod is a plugin with three files, laid out the way the create-a-mod tutorial lays out its own:

worktree-guard/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   └── plugin.json
└── hooks/
    ├── hooks.json
    └── register.js

plugin.json is the plugin manifest. hooks.json points to your code, and its modules key is what makes the plugin a mod. register.js is the code, which the docs call the hooks module. You don't need Node.js or a build step, because Claude Code loads .js and .ts files directly.

When the mod loads, Claude Code calls the register function the file exports and passes it a function named on. Each on call registers a hook for one event. Every hook gets three arguments: $ (the mods API), e (the event, frozen), and next (the rest of the chain, ending in Claude Code's own behaviour). Return next(e) and the tool runs. Return something else without calling next, and you have answered the event yourself.


The worktree is the plot. The mod is the gate.

Write the guard

Create the directories:

mkdir -p worktree-guard/.claude-plugin \
  worktree-guard/hooks worktree-guard/tests

Save the manifest as worktree-guard/.claude-plugin/plugin.json. Don't start the name with claude-: claude plugin validate fails names that look like Anthropic's own.

{
  "name": "worktree-guard",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "description": "Refuses Edit and Write outside the session root"
}

Save the pointer to your code as worktree-guard/hooks/hooks.json. The path is relative to this file:

{
  "description": "worktree-guard hooks module",
  "modules": ["./register.js"]
}

And the guard itself, worktree-guard/hooks/register.js:

// Refuse Edit/Write outside the session's project root
function normalize(p) {
  const out = []
  for (const part of p.split('/')) {
    if (part === '..') out.pop()
    else if (part && part !== '.') out.push(part)
  }
  return '/' + out.join('/')
}

function isInside(root, file) {
  const r = normalize(root)
  const f = normalize(file.startsWith('/') ? file : r + '/' + file)
  return f === r || f.startsWith(r + '/')
}

async function guard($, e, next) {
  const root = await $.session.root()
  if (isInside(root, e.file_path)) return next(e)
  return { deny: `${e.file_path} is outside ${root}. ` +
    'Edit files in this worktree, or ask the user first.' }
}

export function register(on) {
  on('tool.call', { tool: ['Edit', 'Write'] }, guard)
    .catch(async ($, e, next) => {
      if (next.called) return next(e)
      return { deny: 'worktree-guard failed: ' + next.error.kind }
    })
}

{ tool: ['Edit', 'Write'] } is the matcher, a filter. An array matches any value in it, so the hook runs for those two tools only. Both carry their target as e.file_path, the field the events guide reads in its own Edit/Write example.

For the root, the mods API has both $.session.cwd() and $.session.root(). The type declarations describe root() as where the session started, or where /cd or a worktree move took it, and say a shell cd during the session does not move it. That is the boundary you want: start Claude Code in a worktree and the root is that worktree.

The hooks module has no Node.js APIs, so there is no path module to lean on (API docs). normalize folds ., .. and doubled slashes by hand, so /work/app/../main/x.ts becomes /work/main/x.ts before the comparison. The r + '/' in the prefix test stops /work/app-old from passing as a child of /work/app.

Returning { deny } without calling next means the tool never runs and no permission prompt appears. Claude reads the deny text as the tool's result, so write it as an instruction. Claude Code runs its permission check inside next, so the refusal holds in every permission mode, bypassPermissions included.

A hook that throws or times out is skipped, and the edit would go through. The .catch handler makes the guard fail closed: if guard failed before calling next, the edit is refused. The handler has a one-second limit of its own (reference), and if it fails too, the hook is skipped.

Load it and check what it touches

Load the directory for one session, without installing anything:

claude --plugin-dir ./worktree-guard

Type /plugin at the prompt. The overview says a dim line under the tabs gives the count and the names of loaded mods, so this one should read 1 mod active · worktree-guard. If the name is missing, the module didn't load.

Ask Claude to change a file one level up, for example add a comment to the top of ../README.md. The call should come back refused, with your message as the result. An edit inside the folder goes through as usual. Claude Code hot-reloads a --plugin-dir mod when you save a file in it, so you can tweak the deny text without restarting.

Before you share a mod, or install someone else's, read it the way Claude Code does:

claude plugin validate ./worktree-guard

validate runs the same static analysis Claude Code runs at load time, without executing your code. Look at three lines. The hooks: line should list tool.call with its tool filter in braces. The calls: line should list $.session.root and nothing else: no $.fs, no $.process, no $.http. And because this hook can refuse an action, validate prints a gating-hook line saying whether it has a .catch handler. This one does.

That calls: line is your audit. Mods aren't sandboxed: they run with your permissions and can read files, start processes and make network requests through the mods API.

Test it without a session

claude plugin test runs any *.test.ts file in the plugin directory with no session, sign-in or network (test docs). Nothing real answers in a test, so you stub the session root and the tool itself. Save this as worktree-guard/tests/guard.test.ts:

import { expect, test } from 'claude-code/testing'

test('refuses a write outside the root', async ($, on) => {
  on('session.root', () => ({ value: '/work/app' }))
  on('tool.call', () => ({ result: 'ok' }))
  const out = await $.tool.call({
    tool: 'Write',
    file_path: '/work/app/../main/x.ts',
    content: '',
  })
  expect(out.deny).toBeDefined()
})

test('lets an edit inside the root through', async ($, on) => {
  on('session.root', () => ({ value: '/work/app' }))
  on('tool.call', () => ({ result: 'ok' }))
  const out = await $.tool.call({
    tool: 'Edit',
    file_path: '/work/app/src/a.ts',
    old_string: 'a',
    new_string: 'b',
  })
  expect(out).toEqual({ result: 'ok' })
})

A stub for a mods API call is named without the $. and returns { value }. The tool.call stub stands in for Claude Code running the tool, so a call the guard lets through resolves to { result: 'ok' }. Run claude plugin test from the worktree-guard directory; it exits with status 1 on a failure, so it fits in CI. I haven't run this suite myself, so if a field name disagrees with your build, trust the declarations Claude Code writes into .claude-plugin/types/.

Every Hermes task, guarded

The guard gets more useful when every task already has a worktree. I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this section with that in mind. In Hermes, ⌘N (Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows and Linux) starts each task on its own hermes/<name> branch, in its own worktree, with the task as the agent's first prompt. Claude Code runs there as the regular CLI in a real terminal, so a Claude Code session in a Hermes task starts with its root at that task's worktree.


The ⌘N New task sheet in Hermes 2.3.4: Claude Code, the orders-api project, a new hermes/ worktree, Accept edits, and a preview of the claude command Hermes will run.

You can't add --plugin-dir to a command you don't type yourself. For that case Claude Code reads CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS, an environment variable the reference describes as plugin directories "for apps you can't pass a flag to". It takes absolute paths and can live in the env block of ~/.claude/settings.json:

{
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS": "/path/to/mods/worktree-guard"
  }
}

Put the mod somewhere outside your repositories, so no task can rewrite the guard through Edit or Write. From then on, every normal Claude Code session loads the mod, wherever it was started, and an Edit or Write aimed outside the folder Hermes made for the task comes back refused.


The Review Desk's Worktrees tab: one Hermes worktree each for orders-api, web-app and orders-types, with each one's hermes/ branch, task, age and disk size.

One interaction to know about. Since Hermes 2.3.0, a task can include up to 5 extra folders, and those are worked on where they are, on their current branch, not in the task's worktree. The guard will refuse Claude's edits in them. If you use extra folders, add their paths to an allow list in isInside, or leave the guard off for those tasks.

What this mod doesn't stop

It guards two tools by path. It is not a sandbox.

  • Bash. sed -i, cp or echo > into ../app never goes through Edit or Write. Outside bypassPermissions, Claude Code checks output redirects and tee targets against the working directories and asks first. Its sandboxing isolates the Bash commands Claude runs.
  • Other writers. NotebookEdit and MCP tools that write files carry their paths in other fields. Add them to the matcher with the field each one uses.
  • Symlinks. The check compares path strings. A symlink inside the worktree that points outside it passes.
  • Subagents. tool.call fires for subagent calls too. I haven't checked what $.session.root() returns inside a subagent that runs in its own worktree, so test that before you rely on it.
  • POSIX paths only. normalize splits on /. On Windows you would need to handle drive letters and backslashes.

If you'd rather not write JavaScript, a PreToolUse settings hook running a script you already have can block the same calls, and the docs' comparison table recommends exactly that case for settings hooks. What the mod adds is claude plugin test and a validate report anyone can read before loading it.

If this was useful

The hooks module is a plain ES module of async functions, and once you rename it to register.ts and point modules at the new name, the declarations Claude Code writes into .claude-plugin/types/ narrow e as soon as you check e.tool. That is the everyday TypeScript in TypeScript Essentials: types, narrowing, modules and async, across Node, Bun, Deno and the browser. If you write mods, it's the book that makes those type files read like documentation.

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

Start with books 1 and 2. Coming from Kotlin or Java, take book 3 in place of book 1; coming from PHP, book 4. If you ship TypeScript at work, add book 5.

Hermes IDE is free, source-available under BSL 1.1, on macOS, Windows and Linux, and not affiliated with Anthropic or any agent vendor: download it or star it on GitHub.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: I'm 13 and I built a free calorie tracker. It's live, and here's everything that broke.
articles.description: Every calorie app I tried wanted my email and a card before it showed me anything. So I built one...
articles.body_html:
Every calorie app I tried wanted my email and a card before it showed me anything. So I built one that doesn't.

I don't write code by hand. I describe what I want to Google AI Studio and it writes it. Then I test it on my phone, find what's broken, describe the fix. That's the loop. Two weeks of it.

The app is called ForkCount. forkcount.github.io

What it does

It asks your height, weight, age, gender, and activity level. Then it works out your BMR (Mifflin-St Jeor), your TDEE, and a calorie target that keeps you above your BMR floor. If you try to set a target below that line, it shows you the numbers and explains why.

The rest is a food diary, water tracker, weight log, exercise log, weekly meal plan generator, and a community feed. You type "200g chicken and 150g rice" and it parses the food. No card. No trial. No paywall. No email — just a username and password.

Stack

  • React + Vite + TypeScript
  • Firebase Firestore
  • Firebase Auth
  • GitHub Pages, deployed from the docs/ folder
  • No backend. All logic is client-side.

The bug that cost me the most time

Firestore rejects any document that contains an undefined value anywhere inside it. Not null — undefined. And when it fails, it doesn't tell you which field. It just says:

Function setDoc() called with invalid data. Unsupported field value: undefined

If you're saving a nested object with 40 fields, you're searching for a needle in a haystack. I spent days on this. Fix one field, redeploy, same error for a different one.

The fix was a recursive cleaner, routed through every Firestore write:

function cleanForFirestore(obj) {
  if (Array.isArray(obj)) return obj.map(cleanForFirestore);
  if (obj instanceof Date) return obj;
  if (obj && typeof obj === 'object') {
    const out = {};
    for (const k in obj) {
      if (obj[k] !== undefined) out[k] = cleanForFirestore(obj[k]);
    }
    return out;
  }
  return obj;
}

Then I wrapped setDoc, updateDoc, and addDoc in a helper that cleans every write. One import change, and no write in the app can send undefined to Firestore again.

The second bug: GitHub Pages was serving my source files

The site broke with this:

Failed to load module script: Expected a JavaScript-or-Wasm module script but the server responded with a MIME type of "application/octet-stream"

I stared at the code for two days. The problem was in GitHub Pages settings. It was serving my repo root — which has /src/main.tsx — instead of my built dist/ folder. The fix was to copy dist/ into a docs/ folder, point Pages at /docs, and stop letting it serve source.

The error was the browser refusing to run a TypeScript file as JavaScript. Once I knew that, it made sense.

What I'd like feedback on

  • Does the onboarding flow make sense the first time you see it?
  • Is the calorie calculation right? Mifflin-St Jeor for BMR, activity multiplier for TDEE, 300–500 deficit, floor at BMR.
  • Does it break on your phone?

I'm 13 and I built this by directing AI Studio, not by writing code by hand. If something looks like a beginner mistake, it probably is. Tell me and I'll fix it.

forkcount.github.io

articles.title: The Search Engine With Zero Server Calls
articles.description: A prebuilt JSON index, weighted AND matching, ARIA combobox - site search with no server, no dependencies, no round-trips. ~1,000 pages.
articles.body_html:
Every search box you've ever shipped came with the same tax: a search endpoint, a spinner, a payload, and - if you took the SaaS route - a service that bills monthly to index what is usually a few hundred names the page could have shipped with in the first place.

I run The DJ Calendar, a site of roughly 1,000 pages covering DJs, venues and shows. Its site search has never had a server. No endpoint, no spinner waiting on a round-trip, no monthly bill. It's a JSON index rendered into the page at deploy time and a small scoring function that runs in the browser on every keystroke.

I've now extracted that whole pattern into a standalone, MIT-licensed repo: instant-search-index. Zero dependencies. One JS file. This post is how it works and, because that's where the real lessons live, what broke along the way.

The opinion underneath it

Most search boxes are infrastructure cosplay. A request to a search endpoint, a spinner, a payload - for a catalog of a few hundred records.

My stance: if the catalog fits in the page, the search belongs in the page. Ship the index as JSON, score it in the browser on every keystroke, and the search feels instant because it is instant. There is no network left to wait on.

There's a second property I care about even more than speed: the index is generated, not queried. It's built at deploy time by the same PHP that renders the artist pages, so the search index and the page content come from the same data. A search index that drifts from the pages it links to is worse than no search at all - this one can't drift, because it's rendered from the source, not synced to it.

The index contract

One JSON array per page. Three searchable fields, two display-only ones:

{
  "title": "Carl Cox",
  "subtitle": "Techno / House",
  "keywords": "techno house icon ibiza space",
  "badge": "Artist",
  "url": "/artists/carl-cox"
}
  • title - the primary match surface, weighted heaviest
  • subtitle - displayed right-aligned, lightly searchable
  • keywords - the synonym field: genre names, city names, whatever users type that isn't literally in the title
  • badge and url - display only; url is where Enter navigates

The keywords field is the quiet hero. Users type "edm", the record says "Tiësto". The keyword field is where you encode everything a human might type that the title will never contain - and it's also where accent folding happens, because folding happens once at index-build time, in PHP, and the client stays ASCII-simple forever. That's why "tiesto" finds Tiësto and "kolsch" finds Kölsch without a single line of Unicode normalization in the browser.

Scoring: AND semantics, weighted by where the match lands

Every keystroke scores every record. A record must match every query token somewhere, or it drops out - AND semantics, not OR. Type "house mafia" and you get Swedish House Mafia and nothing else.

Where a match lands decides the rank:

Signal Weight Example
Title token, exact 60 "cox" hits Carl Cox
Title token, prefix 40 "ame" hits Ame*lie* Lens
Keyword, exact 30 "techno" hits the genre field
Keyword, prefix 18 "tech" hits "techno"
Subtitle, exact / prefix 12 / 8 useful, not the point
Loose substring 4 the safety net
Full-phrase hit +25 "black coffee" beats token soup

The core of the scorer:

var W = { titleExact: 60, titlePrefix: 40, keywordExact: 30,
          keywordPrefix: 18, subtitleExact: 12, subtitlePrefix: 8,
          substring: 4, phraseBonus: 25 };

function scoreEntry(entry, queryTokens, rawQuery) {
  var total = 0;
  for (var i = 0; i < queryTokens.length; i++) {
    var best = bestFieldScore(entry, queryTokens[i]);
    if (!best) { return 0; }        /* one miss kills the record */
    total += best;
  }
  if (entry.haystack.indexOf(rawQuery) !== -1) { total += W.phraseBonus; }
  /* Shorter titles win ties */
  return total * 1000 - entry.record.title.length;
}

That last line is my favorite trick in the file. Two sort priorities - score, then shorter title - get packed into a single integer: multiply the score by 1000, subtract the title length. No comparator object, no tie-break loop, no second pass. It's arithmetic doing the work of a sort policy.

Ties after that fall to index order, which keeps results stable while you type - the list doesn't reshuffle under your fingers mid-word, and mid-word stability matters more than people think. Type "ame" and watch the list: if entries jump around per keystroke, users stop trusting it.

Tokens are precomputed once at load - per-record token arrays for title, subtitle and keywords - so a keystroke scores prepared arrays and never re-splits a string. On the demo's 99 records that's microseconds per keystroke. You'd need six figures of records before this design complains.

The combobox: keyboard is first-class, not an afterthought

The input is a real ARIA combobox, wired properly:

input.setAttribute("role", "combobox");
input.setAttribute("aria-expanded", "false");
input.setAttribute("aria-controls", listId);
input.setAttribute("aria-autocomplete", "list");

Results live in a role="listbox"; arrow keys move an aria-activedescendant pointer; Enter goes to the active option - and here's the detail I'm proudest of: if a query produces exactly one result, Enter goes straight there. No need to arrow down to the only item on screen. The keyboard path is as short as the mouse path.

Two more details that took iteration:

Escape everything before rendering. Matched text gets wrapped in a mark tag, but the title is escaped first - index entries are data, not markup. If an artist were ever named like a script tag, the search box would display it, not run it.

The debounce is 80ms, not the tutorial's 300. Debounce in most search boxes exists to protect a server you're about to annoy. There's no server here. The 80ms is only there to batch keystrokes into one render; the scoring itself is cheap enough to run on every input event.

What broke

The dropdown that vanished. The search widget was perfect in isolation and invisible in production: the results list rendered inside hero containers with overflow: hidden, which quietly amputated everything below the fold of the header. The fix was overflow: visible on every hero and header parent - and a rule I've repeated since: the search box is rarely where the bug is. The page around the search box is the bug farm.

The AND decision I almost reversed. The instinct is to fall back to OR matching when AND finds nothing: "you searched for X, maybe you meant these loosely related things." I left it out. AND plus an honest "No matches." beats OR plus a wall of tangential results, because the top of the list is the product - a confident zero communicates more than a desperate eight.

The payload, stated honestly. The index ships inside the page, which means the page carries it. Hundreds of records is trivially fine - this is a few kilobytes of JSON. But this pattern has a boundary, and the boundary is not where you'd panic: it's when your catalog stops being "names a human can scan" and starts being "a dataset". At tens of thousands of records, close the laptop and use a real engine. Most sites - including most sites that paid for one - are nowhere near that line.

Extracting it

The repo ships the engine, the CSS, and a demo where you can search the real DJ Mag Top 100 the way the production site does - including a "Show how each result scored" toggle that exposes the actual math behind each ranking. No stand-ins; the demo runs the same engine, the same weights, the same defaults as production.

Usage is one line, either declarative (the index travels in the attribute, the widget builds itself):

<input type="text" data-instant-search='[
  {"title": "Carl Cox", "subtitle": "Techno", "keywords": "techno house icon", "url": "/artists/carl-cox"}
]'>

or programmatic, for records that arrive at runtime:

InstantSearch.attach(inputEl, records, { maxResults: 6 });

The numbers

  • 0 dependencies, 0 server round-trips, 1 JS file
  • ~60 lines of scoring core (320 with comments and the combobox)
  • Microsecond scoring on hundreds of records, per keystroke
  • ARIA combobox semantics, full keyboard navigation, escaped output
  • Running in production across ~1,000 pages since 2015

The pattern is instant-search-index on GitHub, with a live demo - type something, then put the mouse away and use the arrow keys.

articles.title: I built a free GitHub profile README generator with no badge APIs, no backend and a 3D contribution universe
articles.description: Your GitHub profile is often the first thing a recruiter, a hiring manager or a possible collaborator...
articles.body_html:
Your GitHub profile is often the first thing a recruiter, a hiring manager or a possible collaborator sees. For most of us it's a contribution graph and six pinned repos. That's a missed chance.

So I built README-Glassfolio: type your GitHub username, pick a theme, and get a complete profile README with a banner, stats, a contribution heatmap, a 3D "contribution universe", a languages card, a timeline, project cards and Connect buttons. Then publish it to your profile in one click.

👉 Try it: readme-glassfolio.in
⭐ Source (MIT): github.com/SandeepKomal/README-Glassfolio

The problem with most profile README tools

If you've made a fancy profile README before, you've probably pasted in a stack of image URLs pointing at somebody else's server: a stats card here, a streak counter there, a typing banner on top. It looks great until:

  • the free service hits its rate limit and your profile fills with broken images,
  • the service shuts down,
  • or you realise every visit to your profile is pinging a third party.

README-Glassfolio takes a different approach: everything is drawn as plain SVG files that live in your own <user>/<user> repo. No badge APIs, no stats services, no backend. Data comes straight from api.github.com, and every card is rendered in your browser.

What you get

Here's a README made with it (Royal theme, default options), shown on GitHub's dark and light pages:

  • Wave header and footer: a gradient banner with your name, title and top skills, with gently drifting waves.
  • Stats and streak cards: commits, PRs, issues, stars, followers, current and longest streak.
  • Contribution heatmap: laid out like GitHub's own graph, with best day and daily average.
  • 🪐 3D contribution universe: your year as a 3D pie of month wedges round a glowing core, with your top repos orbiting as planets sized by stars, plus a mini pie of your commit / PR / issue / review mix.
  • Languages card, timeline, project cards (pick the ones you want featured, in your order) and Connect buttons.
  • An optional changelog layout that shows your repos as release notes, and a Recently pushed card.

8 themes, or your own colours

aurora, cyber, sunset, emerald, royal, graphite, the light paper, or auto, which picks colours from your username so every profile looks different. Want your brand colours? Choose Custom, pick two accents, and it adjusts them so text stays readable. The tests throw 300 random and extreme colour pairs at it to check that.

Day and night, automatically

By default you get two complete image sets, dark and light, wrapped in <picture> with prefers-color-scheme. Visitors in dark mode see the dark set; visitors in light mode see the light one. Nothing looks out of place on either page.

Publish in one click, and it stays fresh

  1. Create your profile repo (your-username/your-username, public).
  2. Create a fine-grained token limited to only that repo, with Contents and Workflows set to read and write.
  3. On readme-glassfolio.in, enter your username, tweak the options, press Publish to GitHub and paste the token.

All files land in one commit. The token goes only to api.github.com, stays in memory, and is cleared after publishing.

A README is normally a snapshot, so "Keep my stats fresh every day" is on by default. It adds a small GitHub Action to your repo that rebuilds the README once a day and commits only when something changed. It has no uses: lines (no third-party actions), no secrets, one permission (contents: write), and a copy of the generator sits in .readme-patch/ so you can read every line that runs. If GitHub's API is down that day, it changes nothing, so you never end up with a half-empty profile.

Prefer not to use a token? Download the zip and drag the files into your repo.

How often it updates

⚠️ GitHub pauses scheduled workflows after 60 days without activity in a repo. If your profile stops updating, open the Actions tab and re-enable the workflow. It takes one click.

  • README and cards: once a day, at a time worked out from your username, so runs are spread out without anyone setting a cron time. The page shows your time before you publish.
  • 3D universe: every 6 hours, by a second small workflow.
  • Only real changes are committed, so there are no empty commits. Refresh any time with Run workflow in the Actions tab.
  • GitHub caches README images for a few minutes, so a new commit can take a moment to show.

📘 New to profile READMEs? There's a step-by-step guide with screenshots (also as a PDF) that walks through every click.

Safe to paste a token into

I took security seriously, because I'm asking people to paste a token into a web page:

  • A strict Content-Security-Policy: scripts only from the site itself, network requests only to the site and api.github.com, no inline scripts, no eval.
  • No innerHTML anywhere. The live preview builds elements from a whitelist, so markup hidden in a bio or repo description can't do anything.
  • Tokens are never stored and can't end up in a share link.
  • The browser tests actually attack the page (injected scripts, inline handlers, eval, fetch/XHR/image/iframe/WebSocket to another host) and check that everything is blocked.

For terminal fans: there's a CLI

Same engine, zero dependencies, Node 18+:

git clone https://github.com/SandeepKomal/README-Glassfolio
cd README-Glassfolio

node cli.js your-username --theme cyber --role "Cloud Engineer" --stack "AWS, Terraform"
node cli.js --sample                       # try it with no network
GITHUB_TOKEN=github_pat_xxx node cli.js your-username --publish --daily

Output goes to ./out/: README.md, banner.svg and cards/.

A few small touches I'm proud of

  • A preview that tells the truth. It shows your README inside a mock GitHub profile at GitHub's real widths (896px desktop, 390px phone), with light/dark switching.
  • Text that always fits. A fuzz tool renders about 1,800 cards with extreme repo names (90 characters, million-star counts) in a real browser and measures every text box so nothing collides.
  • Motion that respects people. Animations are plain CSS inside the SVGs. With "reduce motion" on, visitors see the finished still image.
  • Share links like ?user=octocat&theme=cyber rebuild the same setup, and a 1280×640 share image is ready for LinkedIn or X.
  • A "Make it even better" checklist scores your profile and points to what's missing.

Try it and tell me what you think

It's free, open source (MIT), and runs entirely in your browser:

  • 🌐 Web app: readme-glassfolio.in
  • 💻 GitHub: SandeepKomal/README-Glassfolio

If you make your profile with it, drop your GitHub link in the comments. I'd love to see what themes people pick. A ⭐ on the repo helps more developers find it, and issues and PRs are welcome. Next on my list is a compact card design that reads better on phones.

Happy profile-polishing! ✨

articles.title: Transparência de Tributos dos Combustíveis: do PDF da Fecombustíveis ao XML do PDV, sem servidor
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle           O...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

O que eu construí

Todo posto de combustível no Brasil precisa mostrar na nota/cupom quanto do preço é imposto (Lei 12.741/2012, a "Lei da Transparência"). Para combustíveis, os valores de ICMS, PMPF e PIS/COFINS mudam por estado e por mês, e a referência que todo mundo usa é o PDF "Carga tributária estadual" publicado pela Fecombustíveis.

O problema: alguém precisa abrir esse PDF todo mês, conferir 27 UFs × 6 combustíveis e redigitar tudo no arquivo TransparenciaTributos.xml que o sistema de PDV lê. É trabalho chato, manual e fácil de errar.

O Transparência de Tributos – Combustíveis automatiza isso:

  • a cada 8 horas um workflow do GitHub Actions procura o PDF novo no site da Fecombustíveis;
  • uma IA lê o PDF e devolve os valores por combustível e UF;
  • o sistema compara com o XML do mês anterior, destaca o que mudou e confere as contas (PMPF × alíquota = ICMS; PMPF × 9,25% = PIS/COFINS no GNV);
  • gera o XML novo — fechando o bloco antigo no dia anterior e abrindo um bloco novo de vigência só para os combustíveis que mudaram;
  • publica tudo e avisa por e-mail e Discord.

Quem pagaria por isso? Software houses de automação comercial que atendem postos (como a Imex Tecnologia, onde isso nasceu) e redes de postos que hoje fazem essa atualização na mão. É um nicho pequeno, específico e com uma dor recorrente todo mês — exatamente o tipo de "side hustle" que vira serviço por assinatura.

Demo

  • Gerador do XML: https://imextecnologia.github.io/tributacao/
  • Tributos por estado (atualiza sozinha a partir do XML mais recente): https://imextecnologia.github.io/tributacao/tributos.html

Código

imextecnologia / tributacao

tributacao

Transparência de Tributos – Combustíveis

Site estático (GitHub Pages) que gera todo mês o XML TransparenciaTributos a partir do PDF "Carga tributária estadual" da Fecombustíveis.

Site: https://imextecnologia.github.io/tributacao/ · Tributos por estado: https://imextecnologia.github.io/tributacao/tributos.html

Como funciona

  1. Busca do PDF – a cada 8 horas um workflow procura o PDF novo na página da Fecombustíveis, salva em pdf/ e já gera o XML do mês em xml/ (veja Busca automática do PDF).
  2. Leitura com IA – o site envia o PDF ao Google Gemini, que devolve os valores por combustível e UF.
  3. Comparação – os valores são comparados com o XML do mês anterior (em xml/) e o que mudou fica destacado.
  4. Geração – para cada combustível que mudou, o bloco antigo termina no dia anterior (ex.: 30/09/2026) e é criado um bloco novo (ex.: 01/10/2026 até 01/01/2050). Combustíveis sem mudança ficam como estão Também é possível baixar uma planilha…
View on GitHub

Como eu construí

  • Site 100% estático no GitHub Pages — HTML + JS puro, sem framework e sem servidor próprio. Tudo roda no navegador.
  • GitHub Actions — buscar-pdf.yml roda às 00:00, 08:00 e 16:00 UTC, baixa o PDF, gera o XML com scripts/gerar-xml.js (mesmas regras do site) e faz commit; pages.yml publica a cada push.
  • Leitura do PDF com IA — hoje o projeto usa o Google Gemini (plano gratuito), com fallback entre gemini-flash-latest, gemini-flash-lite-latest, gemini-2.5-flash e gemini-2.5-flash-lite.
  • Validação antes de confiar na IA — se algum valor não fecha a conta, o XML não é gravado automaticamente; ele fica para revisão humana no site (amarelo = mudou, borda vermelha = conta não fecha). O resultado da IA fica em cache no navegador e, se o XML do mês já existe, a IA nem é chamada.

O que fiz nesta semana (12 a 18 de outubro)

A Fecombustíveis publicou uma atualização no meio do mês (10/10), além do PDF de 01/10. Isso expôs um bug: a página inicial só procurava o XML com a data exata do PDF (20261001) e ignorava o 20261010.

  • 13/10 — corrigi index.html para usar o XML mais recente a partir da data do PDF, comparando-o com o XML anterior a ele, sem chamar a IA de novo. Em tributos.html, o link do PDF passou a apontar para o PDF mais recente até a data do XML (já que uma atualização no meio do mês pode não ter PDF próprio).
  • 13/10 — subi os PDFs/XMLs novos e ajustei o TransparenciaTributos_20261001.xml.
  • 15/10 — revisei e atualizei o TransparenciaTributos_20261010.xml.

Pequeno no diff (+11/−8 linhas), mas é o tipo de caso real que só aparece quando o sistema está rodando em produção.

Por que inovação aberta importa?

Vou ser transparente (o projeto se chama assim, afinal): o modelo que uso hoje não é open-weight — é o Gemini via API. O que é aberto aqui é todo o resto: o código, as regras de geração do XML, os workflows e o histórico de cada XML mensal, públicos no GitHub, para qualquer posto ou software house auditar ou reaproveitar.

E justamente por estar tudo aberto e desacoplado, a IA é uma peça trocável: a extração é uma única chamada que devolve JSON, e a validação das contas é feita fora do modelo. O próximo passo natural é testar um modelo open-weight (como o Gemma) nessa etapa, para não depender do plano gratuito de um provedor e poder rodar localmente. Como o PDF da Fecombustíveis é público, privacidade não é o problema — custo e independência de fornecedor são.

articles.title: Calendar Invites Without OAuth: Five Things That Bit Us
articles.description: Our Slack bot introduces two people and asks them to have a coffee. The obvious next step is putting...
articles.body_html:
Our Slack bot introduces two people and asks them to have a coffee. The obvious next step is putting that meeting in their calendars, and the obvious way is the Google Calendar API: per-user OAuth, a consent screen, refresh tokens to store and revoke, and the same work again for Microsoft.

We shipped it without any of that: a Google template URL and an .ics download, both built on the server and carried in the message. The person clicking creates the event in their own calendar, so we hold no tokens and ask for no access. Here is what that costs, and the five things that bit us.

Why not just call the API

Reading free and busy times is a second identity system. Our only sign-in is Slack. Calendar access would mean per-user consent for two providers, stored third-party refresh tokens (a materially larger thing to protect than anything else we hold) and a new paragraph in the privacy policy. It also only pays off once both people in a pair have connected. Below that it degrades to a link with a suggested time, which is exactly what we built. So we built that first and kept the option.

1. Leaving the time out does not leave the time blank

Google's template URL takes the event as query parameters:

https://calendar.google.com/calendar/render
  ?action=TEMPLATE
  &text=Coffee chat with Dana
  &dates=20260922T130000Z/20260922T133000Z
  &details=Paired by CoffeeSlack
  &add=dana@example.com

We assumed omitting dates would open the editor with an empty time. Tested against a real calendar, it does not: Google pre-fills the next slot from "now", one hour long. A click at around 21:00 on a Friday was offered a Friday coffee at 21:30. A default you choose beats the one Google chooses, so we always send a slot, which is what dragged time zones into a feature that looked like it could avoid them.

2. A Z timestamp renders in each reader's own zone

We sent dates=20260922T130000Z/20260922T133000Z and opened it in a browser two hours ahead of UTC. It rendered as 15:00 to 15:30, with the 30-minute length intact. That is one URL that is correct for both people in a pair even in different countries. The time zone we look up is only ever used to pick a reasonable hour: an unknown zone degrades the suggestion, it never makes the link wrong.

3. Turning 14:00 local into an instant takes two passes

To offer "2pm in their own time" you need the moment at which the clock in some zone reads 14:00. The tempting version reads the offset once:

const guess = Date.UTC(year, month - 1, day, 14, 0);
return guess - offsetAt(guess, zone);   // wrong near a DST change

Treating the wall time as UTC can land the guess on the far side of a daylight-saving change from the real moment, so the offset you read is the other one. Resolving twice fixes it:

const first = guess - offsetAt(guess, zone);
return guess - offsetAt(first, zone);

Searching all 418 zones for a disagreement between the two versions found exactly three: Pacific/Auckland, Pacific/Chatham and Antarctica/McMurdo (which runs on New Zealand time, and which we missed the first time). All at 14:00, and only on the two Saturdays in 2026 when their clocks change. Our slot rule never returns a Saturday, so the bug could not be reached. We kept the second pass anyway, because the defect belongs to the helper, not to the rule that happens to dodge it.

Two smaller things in the same corner. Asking for an unknown zone throws, and the zone name comes from someone's chat profile, so it needs a try and a fallback. And some builds render midnight as hour 24, which quietly shifts a date by a day unless you take it modulo 24.

4. The .ics line limit is 75 octets, not 75 characters

RFC 5545 says a line should not exceed 75 octets, and a continuation begins with a single space or tab. Counting characters instead of bytes works on every name you will test with and breaks on the first one written in Cyrillic or containing an emoji, which arrives cut in half. Walk back off the UTF-8 continuation bytes before you split:

while (end > start && end < bytes.length
       && (bytes[end] & 0xc0) === 0x80) end -= 1;

The leading space on a continuation costs an octet too, so every chunk after the first gets 74.

Escaping has an order: the backslash goes first, or you escape the backslashes you just introduced. Then semicolon, comma, and newline to a literal backslash-n. And the trap we actually shipped into a branch: in JavaScript '\;' is not an escaped semicolon, it is a semicolon. The line that looked like it escaped them compiled, ran and did nothing, so a name like Smith; Jane would have broken the property in two. A linter caught it. The test we had written did not, because it asserted against a string built with the same mistake. Two wrongs agreeing is the normal way this survives review. The fix was to assert by character code instead of writing the expected value as a literal.

Finish with CRLF between every line and one at the end. Outlook is the client that minds.

5. Where you put the token decides who logs it

A calendar client fetches the file with no headers we control, so the URL itself has to be the credential. The first version put the token in the path:

/calendar/coffee.ics/<token>     first version
/calendar/coffee.ics?token=...   second version

We moved it because two pieces of our own code already had an opinion. Our request log records the path and drops the query, under a comment saying the query string can carry secrets. Our error reporter redacts query parameters named token, and only query parameters. A token in the path would have been written to our log on every fetch and shipped to the error reporter on every 5xx. A reviewer found it; the author did not.

And that was still not enough. Our platform writes its own request log. The application never sees it and cannot configure it, and on Cloud Run the field it records is the full URL including the query string. So the token we had just moved into the query was sitting in that log on every fetch: 104 of them, in clear text, behind a fix that had been reviewed and merged as complete. Nothing leaked. Every one of those fetches was our own probing, all in the hour after the deploy and before the first real link went out. We know that from the timestamps rather than the status codes, because the rate limiter answers before the token is read, so a 429 never tells you whether the token was valid.

The repair is a logging exclusion, because the platform can drop a matching entry but cannot redact a field inside one. Two things worth carrying:

  • Anchor the match. Our first filter matched the path as a substring, so anyone could suppress their own log entry by hanging that string off the end of any other URL: a tool for hiding from the logs, shipped as a security fix. Anchor on host and path, and test that a crafted URL fails to match.
  • Know what the exclusion costs. The platform log was the only copy of the client address, user agent and response size. On a public route those are exactly the fields you want when something goes wrong. If it starts to matter, log them yourself from inside the route, where you can leave the secret out on purpose.

The general shape is the part worth keeping: your logging and error reporting encode a belief about which half of a URL is secret, and it is usually right. Your platform holds its own belief, it is usually simpler, and it has not read your comments.

What we deliberately left out

  • No ATTENDEE, ORGANIZER or METHOD in the .ics. Depending on the client, ATTENDEE reads as an invitation or as an ordinary appointment, and it puts a colleague's address in a file in a Downloads folder. Inviting the other person is the Google link's job, where the person clicking is the one inviting.
  • No signature on the token. The identifier carries 48 bits from a random-bytes call, so forging one means guessing those bits. An HMAC adds a secret to rotate and forget (ours sat unset for 26 days once) while protecting nothing: the only person who benefits from forging a pair member's copy is the pair's other member, who was sent the same details anyway.
  • No availability lookup. That needs the API, which needs the OAuth, which is the project we did not do. The slot we suggest is a guess both people are expected to move.

When this is the wrong approach

Everything above depends on a person being there to click. If you need to know when someone is free, or to put an event in their calendar while they are asleep, none of this helps and you are back to the API and the consent screen. What it buys is the 80 percent case at none of the cost, and the option to do the rest later.

The Google behaviour described here was checked against a live calendar on 21 September 2026. It is not documented anywhere we could find, so it can change without warning. Check it yourself before relying on it.

This is the bot it went into: CoffeeSlack pairs teammates for a coffee chat in Slack. Free for every team, no card.
